steps.result_caption: Looking back, then away, then back again with a smile — inside a single unbroken take, and none of it requested.

steps.title: The 4K claim checks out — and the glance is the shot
steps.text: This one survives inspection where other files in this library did not: the archived master really is 3840×2160, and the delivery is 1920×1080 H.264 at 24 fps, 10.10s, 3.4 MB with a 128 kbit AAC bed, small enough to preload instantly. No sharpening pass was added on the way down, which is why the haze still reads as air rather than as noise. And the editorial point: the second glance at 0:06 is the only moment in ten seconds where anything happens. If you are cutting this into a doc opener, that smile is your in-point — not the clean walk-away frames the brief was written to produce.
steps.result_caption: The turn, the smile, the walk away again. Three seconds of the only thing in the clip an editor can build on.

guides.result: 10.10 seconds of usable documentary b-roll in one unbroken take — the look delivered exactly as written, and a reminder that a following camera is never invisible to whoever the model puts in front of it.

guides.title: Restyle a physics-driven testimonial widget
guides.desc: Take a third-party Three.js testimonial widget (rope-physics puller, canvas-textured cards) and rebuild its whole visual language — CSS tokens, stage lighting, card typography and copy — to match the Quadcode dark UI, without touching the underlying rig.

steps.title: 1. Audit the source before touching anything
steps.text: The original repo ships a warm cream/terracotta editorial theme: Georgia serif headline, #C2603C terracotta accent, paper-grain canvas cards. None of it is Quadcode — but the rig underneath (rope physics, drag-to-scroll, canvas-painted cards) is solid and worth keeping untouched.
steps.prompt: Clone the target repo, run it locally, and list every hardcoded visual value: CSS custom properties, font-family declarations, and any hex colors baked into the JS (canvas fill styles, Three.js material colors, light colors). Do not touch logic yet — only inventory.
steps.result_caption: The starting state before any edit — this is what the audit was run against.

steps.title: 2. Swap CSS tokens for the Quadcode dark system
steps.text: Replace the :root palette wholesale: cream/terracotta becomes bg #0E0E14 / bg-2 #1A1A24, text goes white with rgba-based muted tiers, and the single accent becomes the acc-1→acc-2 orange-to-red gradient (#FF9569 → #DD344D). Serif headline swaps for Space Grotesk, body for Manrope — both pulled from Google Fonts, matching the rest of the guide site.
steps.prompt: Rewrite the :root CSS variables to the Quadcode dark token set (bg, bg-2, ink, ink-soft, line, acc-1, acc-2). Replace the serif display font with Space Grotesk and the system-UI body font with Manrope. Re-point every button, pill, dot and progress indicator that referenced the old single terra color onto the new two-stop gradient instead of a flat fill.

steps.title: 3. Repaint the canvas card texture — one instruction landed half right
steps.text: The testimonial cards are canvas-drawn textures wrapped onto a 3D plane, not DOM elements — so the paper-cream gradient, grain, quote-serif and avatar-initial styling all had to be repainted directly in the paintCard() function. Stage lighting got the full pass asked for: hemisphere/key/fill retuned for a dark studio, rim light now accent-orange (#FF9569). "Recolor avatar rings and star ratings to the new accent palette" split down the middle: star ratings are the accent orange as asked, but the avatar mark is a filled disc (no ring), and it keeps each person's own random tint — 12 different colors, only 2 of which are actually brand orange/red. A rainbow of arbitrary label colors reads as random, not branded — check it after the fact.
steps.prompt: Inside the canvas-texture paint routine, replace the paper-gradient background, grain color and quote-serif font with the dark bg gradient, Space Grotesk headline font and Manrope body font. Recolor avatar rings and star ratings to the new accent palette. Retune HemisphereLight/DirectionalLight intensities and colors so the stage reads as a dark studio, with the rim light carrying the brand accent color.
steps.result_caption: Canvas grain on the cards and the retuned key light. Compare with the frame under step 1.

steps.title: 4. Replace the testimonial copy — asked for six, got twelve
steps.text: The prompt asks for six quotes across six named roles (Game Dev, Product Designer, Motion Designer, QA Engineer, Founder, Design Lead). What shipped is twelve — DATA has 12 entries, 12 dots on the rope. Only three of the six requested roles show up at all (Senior Game Developer, Senior Product Designer, Senior Motion Designer); QA Engineer, Founder and Design Lead never appear. The other nine slots are roles nobody asked for (Product Lead, Lead UI/UX Designer, Engineering Lead, Technical Artist, Senior Frontend Engineer, Brand Designer, a startup CTO, an ML Engineer, a Creative Director). The "references a specific guide" instruction also didn't survive contact: Marcus Chen's line just says "last NPC went from brief to in-engine in an afternoon" — no guide named — and Dev Raman's motion quote never mentions a guide at all. What's genuinely good: every quote still tells a concrete before/after story instead of generic praise, it just tells twice as many of them as briefed.
steps.prompt: Replace the DATA testimonials array with six English-language quotes attributed to roles relevant to a design/dev guide platform (Game Dev, Product Designer, Motion Designer, QA Engineer, Founder, Design Lead). Each quote must reference a concrete detail — a specific guide, a specific failure that was fixed, a specific number — not generic praise. Update the section eyebrow and headline to match.
steps.result_caption: Cards cycling with the new English copy and Quadcode-guide roles.

steps.title: 5. Ship it live — drag the rope right here
steps.text: Not a screen recording — the actual restyled widget, embedded live below via iframe. Drag the rope down (or press the arrows) to pull the next card in; the physics, drag-to-scroll and card-swap logic are all untouched from the original repo — only the visual system and copy changed.

guides.result: The same rope-physics testimonial rig, now running the Quadcode dark visual system end to end — CSS tokens, fonts, and stage lighting all match exactly as briefed, embedded and playable directly in this guide. Two spots where the model didn't follow instructions precisely: the avatar mark keeps a 12-color rainbow instead of the accent palette (stars did get recolored correctly), and the copy pass shipped 12 testimonials across 12 roles instead of the 6 requested — with 3 of the 6 named roles missing entirely. Worth a manual pass on both before calling either one done.

guides.title: Direct a GTA-style skate line in one continuous shot
guides.desc: Create a 15-second night skate run with grounded board physics, a close chase camera and a reactive trick HUD.

steps.title: 1. Build a line, not a montage — the wardrobe and the cut didn't listen
steps.text: The ground delivers: it's genuinely wet, and city lights reflect off the concrete in every frame. The rest of this prompt gets ignored. "Red tracksuit" comes back as a black crewneck top over dark maroon trousers — two unrelated colors, no tracksuit silhouette, and nothing red. "One continuous 16:9 shot" doesn't hold either: there's a hard scene cut at 13.9s (scene-detect score 0.12) where the camera jumps to a tighter, lower angle for the final 1.2 seconds. Wet ground and chase-camera geometry are the only two promises this line kept.
steps.prompt: Third-person open-world game footage at a wet industrial skate plaza at night. Male skater in a red tracksuit rides toward a low concrete ledge. Close chase camera behind and slightly below shoulder height, city lights reflecting on wet ground, one continuous 16:9 shot.
steps.result_caption: Wet concrete, reflections, chase camera in position — and a black top over maroon trousers that is not the red tracksuit the prompt asked for.

steps.title: 2. Protect board-to-foot contact — it grinds, then it breaks
steps.text: The prompt asks for one clean ollie over a ledge. What's on screen through 0:02–0:06 is a rail grind: feet planted, board balanced flat along the top edge of a concrete ledge — a different trick entirely, never an airborne ollie. The real failure comes right after, at 6.8–7.8s, exactly the window this step exists to protect: the board detaches from the feet and, while it's floating free, changes color three times in one second — lime-green at 6.8s, magenta at 7.2s, dark purple at 7.4s, back to green at 7.6s, purple again at 7.8s. That's not just a physics miss, it's the renderer losing track of which object the board even is. By 8–9.6s it's recovered — single-colored board, feet back on it, knees compressing on landing — so the fix holds on touchdown, it just doesn't survive the trick itself.
steps.prompt: The skater compresses, pops one clean ollie over the ledge and lands with both feet planted over the trucks. Board remains rigid and connected to the rider, wheels contact the ground together, knees absorb impact, no impossible flips or limb distortion.
steps.result_caption: This is a rail grind, not the ollie the prompt asked for — feet are planted here, but the board detaches and flickers through three colors one second later, at 6.8–7.8s.

steps.title: 3. Let the HUD confirm the trick — wrong corner, frozen number
steps.text: The minimap lands exactly where asked, bottom-left, with a speed readout the prompt didn't even request ("31 KM/H · WET CONCRETE · TRACTION 82%"). Everything about trick name and score is off. They sit bottom-right, not top-right, as a static "BOARDSLIDE · KICKFLIP · WALLRIDE" checklist that never names the move actually performed and never changes. Top-right — the corner that was supposed to hold the trick name and score — is spent on a TIME/CASH readout and, underneath it, an actual Grand Theft Auto VI logo, neither of which appears anywhere in the prompt. And the one instruction with a trigger condition fails outright: checked at twelve timestamps from 0s to 15s, including 9s where the landing happens, "LINE SCORE" reads 24,850 and the multiplier reads x4.0 in every single frame. Only a decorative combo bar creeps from 30% to 75% full and then drops back to 35% by the end — animated, but disconnected from the number sitting right next to it.
steps.prompt: Add a restrained game HUD: circular minimap bottom-left, trick name and score top-right, small balance or speed indicator. The score updates immediately after the landing and all UI remains locked to screen coordinates.
steps.result_caption: Trick name and score sit bottom-right, not top-right — top-right instead holds an uninvited Grand Theft Auto VI logo. The score itself (24,850 x4.0) is identical in every frame of the clip.

steps.title: 4. Cut on the roll-away — right idea, wrong duration
steps.text: Container specs are exact: 1920×1080, H.264, 24fps, stereo AAC at 44.1kHz, 15.046s total. The edit math is off, though. The board settles back under the rider around 9s, so the roll-away actually runs about six seconds, not the two the step describes — and it isn't even one continuous roll-away: a hard cut at 13.9s hands the last 1.2 seconds to a different, tighter shot. The clip does end past the trick instead of on it, which is the part worth keeping. The "two seconds" and "one line" framing overstates how clean the tail actually is.
steps.prompt: Deliver a 15-second 1920 × 1080 H.264 clip at 24 fps with stereo audio and web fast-start.
steps.result_caption: 1920×1080/24fps/stereo AAC all check out — but this excerpt starts after a hard cut at 13.9s, inside a second shot, not the tail of one continuous take.

guides.result: The container spec, wet-ground look and landing recovery are real. The rest is staged: the "ollie" on screen is a rail grind, the actual airborne moment detaches the board and flickers it through three colors, the HUD's trick name and score sit in the wrong corner behind an uninvited Grand Theft Auto VI logo, and the score itself never updates from 24,850 across all 15 seconds.

guides.title: Direct a GTA-style surf stunt with a playable HUD
guides.desc: Build a 15-second open-world surf clip where the wave physics, chase camera and game interface all sell the same playable moment.

steps.title: 1. Frame it like gameplay — it delivered the drone angle it argued against
steps.text: This step's own case is that a "beautiful drone angle would weaken the idea" and asks instead for a chase camera two metres behind and slightly above the surfer. What's on screen is the opposite: a wide, elevated, distant establishing shot with the rider occupying a small fraction of the frame — closer to a cliff-top drone view of the cove than a close third-person chase. There's no minimap, no health bar and no mission marker in this footage at all — that HUD description belongs to a different guide's render, not this one.
steps.prompt: Third-person open-world game footage of a male surfer riding a turquoise wave through a rocky tropical cove at sunset. Camera follows two metres behind and slightly above the character, wide 16:9 frame, realistic game-engine lighting, continuous shot.
steps.result_caption: This is the wide, elevated "drone angle" the step's own text argues against — not a close chase camera two metres behind the rider.

steps.title: 2. Give the wave one readable line — the board leaves the rider mid-air
steps.text: "Board stays attached to both feet" is the one hard rule in this prompt, and it breaks at 8.0s: the surfer goes airborne off the wave around 7.6s, and by 8.0s the board is tumbling alone in frame with no rider visible anywhere near it, for a full 0.8 seconds (8.0–8.4s) before he reappears crouched on it in the water at 8.6s. That's not a wobble, it's a complete separation the model never explains — he isn't shown falling, swimming or being thrown; he simply isn't in the shot while his board is. The carve itself before and after that gap is genuinely clean: one wave face, one spray fan, no competing swell.
steps.prompt: The surfer shifts weight naturally, cuts across the wave face and throws a clean fan of white spray. Board stays attached to both feet, knees absorb the water movement, wave direction remains consistent and the shoreline advances smoothly.
steps.result_caption: This excerpt ends before the failure: at 8.0–8.4s, just past this window, the board tumbles alone with the rider gone from frame entirely.

steps.title: 3. Add HUD elements that react — nothing does
steps.text: Placement is half right: the location label ("VOLCANIC COVE · NORTH BREAK") sits top-left as asked, and the score sits bottom-right as asked. But the bottom-left circle isn't a minimap — it's a speedometer dial labelled "SURF SPEED", no map, no location markers. And top-right, the corner the prompt never mentioned, carries a TIME/CASH readout and an actual Grand Theft Auto VI logo. None of it reacts: checked across eleven timestamps from 0s to 15s spanning the airborne trick at 7–8s, the speed dial reads exactly "28 KM/H" and the needle sits at the same angle in every frame, and "LINE SCORE" reads 18,750 with an x3.0 multiplier in every one of them too. The interface is sharp and stable, which was asked for — it's also completely static, which wasn't.
steps.prompt: Add a restrained open-world game HUD: circular minimap bottom-left, speed and score bottom-right, small location label top-left. Interface stays sharp and stable while speed and score update during the carve. No large menu panels over the action.
steps.result_caption: Location label and score sit where asked. The bottom-left dial is a static speedometer, not a minimap, and reads the same "28 KM/H" here as at 0s and 15s.

steps.title: 4. Keep the best continuous take — this part actually holds
steps.text: Scene-detection across the full 15.046s finds no hard cut above noise level (highest score 0.09, all below the 0.10 cut threshold this project uses) — it genuinely is one uninterrupted take, unlike the skate guide's version of this same step. Container specs match too: 1920×1080, H.264, 24fps. The HUD does stay locked to its corners the whole time, so "interface placement" is fair. guides.title: Turn a wushu performance into a living ink painting
guides.desc: Direct one 15-second martial-arts shot where the fighter’s movement paints a black ink ring and resolves into a Chinese dragon mural.

steps.title: 1. Lock one visual rule — the fighter breaks it herself
steps.text: "The fighter... stay monochrome" is the claim. From the first second she's on screen, she's wearing a bright orange-red sash at her waist — not in the prompt, not black or white, and visible in every frame through the whole performance. "Locked wide camera" doesn't hold either: there's a hard cut at 4.3s (scene-detect score 0.83, far above the 0.10 noise floor) from a full-body wide shot to an extreme close-up on the brush tip between two pagoda roofs. The grey mountains and wet-ink floor are genuinely there, and hold up through the whole piece.
steps.prompt: A cinematic wushu performance inside a vast white ink-wash studio. One female martial artist in a white top and flowing black trousers. Monochrome palette, wet black sumi ink, soft grey mountains in the distance, locked wide camera, realistic fabric and body mechanics.
steps.result_caption: Wet ink and grey mountains are genuinely monochrome. The orange-red sash at her waist, visible here and in every other frame, is not.

steps.title: 2. Make movement generate the graphic — it's a brush, not her arms
steps.text: The prompt asks for ink following her bare arms as she pivots. What she's actually holding for the entire performance, from 1s onward, is a giant ink-loaded calligraphy brush the size of a staff — she wields it like a weapon and the ink trails from its bristle tip, not from her limbs. That's a real prop the prompt never mentions, and it's the thing actually generating the stroke. Once you accept the brush as the mechanism, the physics of it are convincing: bristle texture, splatter at direction changes, and a ring that closes cleanly on her low stance.
steps.prompt: As she pivots into a low wushu stance, a thick ribbon of wet black ink follows her arms and circles her body. The stroke has visible bristle texture, splatter at direction changes and believable liquid inertia. Keep her face, costume and scale consistent.
steps.result_caption: That's a giant calligraphy brush trailing the ink, not her bare arms as the prompt describes — she carries it the whole way through.

steps.title: 3. Resolve the motion into one payoff — the dragon isn't flat ink anymore
steps.text: The transformation itself works: the ring genuinely expands into the dragon with no cut in between, and it holds on a wide tableau with the fighter small below it, exactly as asked. "Painted ink on paper, not a 3D creature" doesn't survive the reveal — the dragon has glowing red-orange eyes, a lit mouth and ember-like highlights along its body, with volumetric shading that reads as a lit creature in space, not a flat brush painting. That also breaks step 1's monochrome rule a second time, this time in the final image the whole piece builds toward.
steps.prompt: The circular ink stroke expands behind the fighter and resolves into a monumental hand-painted Chinese dragon mural. The dragon remains painted ink on paper, not a 3D creature. End on a balanced wide tableau with the fighter centered below it, no text and no camera cut.
steps.result_caption: One continuous transformation, no cut — but the glowing red eyes and volumetric shading read as a lit 3D creature, not ink painted flat on paper.

steps.title: 4. Remove drift from the final seconds — this one checks out
steps.text: The container specs are exact: 1920×1080, H.264, 24fps, 15.07s total. The tail genuinely holds — frames from 13s to 15s show the same composition settled with no jitter, and the zoom from the dragon's head to the wide tableau in the seconds before it is one smooth continuous move, not a cut (scene-detect stays under 0.16 the whole way, versus 0.83 at the one real cut earlier in the piece). This is the most literally accurate step in the guide.
steps.prompt: Export a 15-second 16:9 master. Preserve the original sound design, remove unstable tail frames and encode H.264 with web fast-start.
steps.result_caption: The dragon holds steady with no drift from 13s to 15s — the one claim in this guide that measures exactly as described.

guides.result: The transformation itself — ring into dragon, no cut, smooth zoom to the wide tableau — is genuinely well built. The monochrome rule it's built on breaks twice: an orange-red sash on the fighter from frame one, and glowing red eyes on the dragon at the payoff. The mechanism is a giant ink-brush, not her bare arms, and there's one hard cut at 4.3s the "locked wide camera" instruction didn't survive. Format and final-seconds stability are exactly as specified.

guides.title: The model did the arithmetic and got the geometry wrong
guides.desc: A parametric kitchen configurator built end to end. GPT-Image invented a weighted decision matrix with twelve scores and computed all three totals correctly — from a 171-character prompt containing no numbers. Then it drew the "orthographic" dimension sheet at six different scales, and Meshy returned all six modules normalised to the same 1.90-unit height. Measured, not eyeballed.

steps.title: It invented twelve scores and added them up correctly
steps.text: The prompt below is 171 characters and contains no numbers at all — no weights, no scores, no totals. What came back: four criteria weighted 35 / 20 / 30 / 15, summing to exactly 100%; twelve individual scores; and three weighted totals. Check the arithmetic by hand and all three are exact to two decimals. Grid-Snap: 5×0.35 + 4×0.20 + 5×0.30 + 3×0.15 = 4.50. Rigid Presets: 4×0.35 + 5×0.20 + 4×0.30 + 5×0.15 = 4.35. Freeform: 2×0.35 + 3×0.20 + 2×0.30 + 4×0.15 = 2.50. Nothing was corrected afterwards. This is the thing to take from the guide: the model is reliable when the output is a self-consistent number system, and everything downstream in this project failed in exactly the opposite way.
steps.prompt: GOAL: Decision-matrix sheet comparing Grid-Snap / Freeform / Rigid Presets against 4 weighted criteria, with floor-plan icon per strategy and a locked scoring rule footer.
steps.result_label: The delivered sheet · every total re-computed by hand
steps.result_caption: Grid-Snap 4.50, Rigid Presets 4.35, Freeform 2.50 — all three verify against the printed weights. The 0.15 margin between the top two is real, which is why the pitch rule got written into the footer instead of left to memory.

steps.title: The "orthographic" sheet is drawn at six different scales
steps.text: Same model, same session, one step later. The labels are correct — every width is a multiple of 300mm, the drawer stack at 300 really is the narrowest. The drawing is not. Measure the white dimension lines in pixels and divide by the printed millimetres and you get six different scales on one sheet: base cabinet 0.390 px/mm, wall cabinet 0.372, drawer stack 0.450, corner unit 0.311, island 0.302, appliance bay 0.223. That is a 2.0× spread. The drawer stack is labelled half the width of the base cabinet and drawn at 58% of it; the appliance bay is labelled 2100mm tall and drawn 314px against the base cabinet's 239px for 720mm — it should be 697px. Three modules share a printed 720mm height and, to the sheet's credit, all three are drawn at exactly 239px. Everything else is decoration. Treat a generated spec sheet as a labelled diagram, never as a drawing you can scale off.
steps.prompt: GOAL: Orthographic module-library sheet, 3×2 grid, 6 kitchen modules with dimension lines and W×D×H spec line each, same OAK/GRAPHITE/STEEL palette as the identity render.
steps.result_label: The delivered sheet · dimension lines measured in pixels
steps.result_caption: Top row heights agree (239px each for 720mm). Widths do not: 234px and 223px both labelled 600mm, 135px labelled 300mm. The bottom row runs on a third and fourth scale again.

steps.title: One of the six meshes came back the right shape — try it live
steps.text: Meshy returned all six modules with their longest axis between 1.8959 and 1.8996 units. Not similar — normalised. The 300mm pitch the whole project is built on does not exist in the files. Check the proportions instead of the absolute size and only the wall cabinet survives: measured 2.059 : 1.752 : 1.000 against 2.057 : 1.714 : 1.000 for the briefed 600×350×720. The drawer stack — the module that defines the pitch — should read 2.400 : 2.000 : 1.000 and comes back 1.659 : 1.357 : 1.000. The island's two equal dimensions hold to within 1.5% but its long axis is 26% short. So every mesh needs rescaling by hand before it can be placed, and a viewer will not show you this, because model-viewer auto-frames each file to fill the canvas. Two more things worth knowing before you download: the prompt asked for quad topology and glTF cannot store quads, so what shipped is 8.2k triangles per module; and 5.5 MB of each 9 MB file is a single uncompressed PNG normal map — 53 MB across six modules, which is why the inspector below takes a moment on first click. The widget itself is 308 lines of hand-written HTML/CSS/JS with real numbers in it: 44px per 300mm cell, prices €420 / €260 / €340 / €610 / €1,450 / €890, total × 1.08. One honest limitation is visible on the plan — the wall cabinet is 350mm deep but occupies a 2×2 cell block, because 350 is not a multiple of 300. Pitch locks width, not depth.
steps.prompt: GOAL: 6 individual production GLB meshes (quad topology, ENABLE_PBR) built from 6 photoreal single-module studio references, matching the step-3 identity render palette and the step-4 locked dimensions exactly.

guides.result: A working configurator whose grid logic, prices and collision rules are all hand-written and all correct — sitting on top of six meshes that need manual rescaling and a spec sheet that cannot be scaled off. The model was trustworthy for the numbers and unreliable for the geometry, and it took measurement to tell which was which.

guides.title: A rigging spec no rigger can use — and the sheet that held
guides.desc: The technical handoff sheet is internally flawless: 12,000 + 18,000 + 5,000 tris add up to exactly the 35,000 budget printed in its header. The mesh that shipped alongside it has 493,266 triangles, zero joints out of the promised 68, and its arms hanging straight down instead of the 45° A-pose the sheet draws. One sheet in this pipeline did survive contact with a ruler — the turnaround, to within 1.2%.

steps.title: Every weighted total on the decision sheet is wrong
steps.text: The prompt named five criteria and their weights and asked for per-criterion scores plus weighted totals. What came back looks authoritative: five rows summing to exactly 100%, bar charts, a lock icon on the winner. Then do the arithmetic the sheet itself prints. Variant A: (5×0.30)+(3×0.20)+(4×0.25)+(3×0.10)+(5×0.15) = 4.15, printed 4.25. Variant B: 3.60, printed 3.55. Variant C: 3.95, printed 3.90. Three formulas, three wrong sums — and the model wrote both the formula and the answer, so it disagrees with itself. The saving grace is that the ranking survives: A still beats C still beats B, so the decision the sheet was made to justify is not affected. Worth knowing what "not affected" is worth: a sibling guide in this collection ran the same kind of sheet through the same model and got all three totals exact. You cannot predict which one you are getting. You can only check.
steps.prompt: GOAL: Senior game-concept decision sheet. Score the 3 silhouettes from step 1 against 5 weighted criteria (Authority 30, Threat 25, Magic 20, Readability 15, Mobility 10). Show per-criterion scores, weighted totals, and a verdict row declaring the winner. Swiss editorial layout, dark ink on bone paper.
steps.result_label: The delivered sheet · all three totals re-computed from the printed formulas
steps.result_caption: Weights are correct and sum to 100%. The totals are not: 4.25 / 3.55 / 3.90 printed against 4.15 / 3.60 / 3.95 computed. Ranking unchanged.

steps.title: "Keep proportions identical across views" actually worked
steps.text: This is the instruction most likely to be ignored, and it held. Measure the figure in each of the four panels — dark pixels below luma 110, ignoring the panel labels — and the heights come out 855, 865, 865 and 859 pixels. A 10-pixel spread across four independently drawn views, 1.2% of the mean. Not a copy-paste: the side view genuinely shows a different collar profile and the back view designs the rear collar plane rather than inventing a cape. So the model can hold a proportion lock across separate drawings in one image. What it cannot do is carry that lock into the next tool, which is the whole subject of the next step.
steps.prompt: GOAL: Production turnaround sheet, 4 orthographic views (FRONT, 3/4, SIDE, BACK) of THE COURT PARASITE on warm bone paper #EDE8DF. Keep proportions identical across views, match the identity render palette and collar geometry. Clean line art with flat color fills, labeled view headers.
steps.result_label: The delivered turnaround · figure heights 855 / 865 / 865 / 859 px
steps.result_caption: Measured left to right: FRONT 855, 3/4 865, SIDE 865, BACK 859. Spread 10 px = 1.2% of the mean.

steps.title: The spec sheet is perfect. The mesh matches none of it.
steps.text: Read the sheet first: 35,000 tris in the header, broken down as head/collar 12,000 + coat/body 18,000 + props 5,000. That adds up exactly. It names four engine sockets, a 68-joint skeleton with 4 cloth chains, six FACS action units, 2048×2048 PBR maps, a 220cm scale ruler, and it draws the arms at a proper 45° A-pose. It is the most convincing document in the whole pipeline. Now open the GLB that shipped with it. 493,266 triangles — 14.1× the budget, in a 19.1 MB file. Zero skins, zero joints, zero animations: the entire node graph is two nodes, so the 68-joint skeleton and every FACS target exist only as ink. The bounding box is 0.2965 × 1.0010 × 0.2021 units, a width-to-height ratio of 0.296, which is a figure with its arms hanging down — a real 45° A-pose runs closer to 0.45. Textures are 4096×4096, not 2048. Even the palette drifted: the atlas medians #1B1615 against the locked #120F17, close in value but hue-flipped from blue-leaning to red-leaning, which is why the coat reads warm brown in the viewer instead of void black. Orbit it below and check the collar from behind — that part it got right. Then treat every number on the blueprint as a request you still have to fulfil by hand.
steps.prompt: GOAL: Technical 3D rigging sheet in orthographic A-pose (45° arms). Annotate engine sockets (socket_hand_r, socket_collar_vfx, socket_ring_l, root_ground), joint count 68, poly budget 35k tris, texel density 1024 px/m, FACS targets AU1 AU2 AU4 AU12 AU15 AU25. Blueprint style, precise callouts, no decoration.
steps.result_label: The delivered GLB · 493,266 tris, 0 joints, arms down
steps.result_caption: Drag to orbit. The blueprint it was supposed to satisfy is in the downloads below — compare them line by line.

guides.result: Six concept sheets, one of which holds up under measurement, and a 19.1 MB mesh that needs a full retopo and a rig built from scratch before it is worth anything. The pipeline is real; the handoff document is a drawing of a handoff document.

guides.title: The safety rule survived. The dates did not.
guides.desc: A food-triage motion identity built on one hard constraint: never claim to know whether food is safe. Across 19.09 seconds the model never once broke that rule — no score, no danger icon, and a closing line that reads ORDER, NOT A SAFETY VERDICT. It also produced a package that was opened four days before it was packaged, because it carried the dates forward between frames and quietly changed what one of them meant.

steps.title: A negative brief is the one instruction it never broke
steps.text: The first prompt in this project forbids things instead of requesting them: no freshness analysis, no score, no medical or danger iconography, and every status readable as text plus shape plus colour so meaning never depends on colour alone. Nineteen seconds later, none of that has been violated — no percentage anywhere in the reel, no cross, no warning triangle used as a hazard sign, and the four-state frame closes on the line ORDER, NOT A SAFETY VERDICT in the model's own typesetting. The redundant encoding survived too, and it earned its keep: sample the four lane colours and three of them sit within ΔRGB 26–29 of the hex values in the prompt, but STABLE came back #696763 against the specified #9A9B96 — a distance of 88, a third darker than asked, and the only lane whose colour genuinely missed. It does not matter, because STABLE is also an equals sign and the word STABLE. That is what redundancy is for. If you only take one habit from this guide, take this one: spend the first prompt on what the output must never contain.
steps.prompt: Lock the safety rule: this system organizes known information. It never claims to analyze food, never outputs a score, never uses medical or danger iconography. Every status must be readable as text + shape + color, so meaning never depends on color alone.
steps.result_label: Frame at 0:15.2 · four lanes, three signals each, one honest footer
steps.result_caption: Measured against the brief: USE FIRST #AC3D2D vs #C6382C, USE SOON #B3762C vs #C68A24, CHECK #22528C vs #1755A5 — all within ΔRGB 29. STABLE #696763 vs #9A9B96 is off by 88 and the shape covers for it.

steps.title: Same date, two meanings, four seconds apart
steps.text: Neither prompt supplied a calendar. The collision prompt named one value, 21 JUN, and the capture prompt named none at all. The model invented 14 JUN and 18 JUN, then carried both across into a separately generated frame — genuine continuity, and more than most image models manage. What it dropped was what the numbers meant. At 0:04.6 the torn strips read OPENED 14 JUN, USE BY 18 JUN, BEST BEFORE 21 JUN. At 0:08.4 the same 18 JUN is boxed and labelled PACKAGE DATE, sitting next to OPENED DATE 14 JUN: a yoghurt opened four days before it was manufactured. The registration sheet drifts elsewhere too. The prompt asked for six boxes labelled PRODUCT, USE BY, OPENED, STORAGE, QTY plus a neutral NO SAFETY VERDICT. Seven boxes shipped. Only OPENED and STORAGE kept their labels; PRODUCT became BARCODE, USE BY became PACKAGE DATE, QTY became WEIGHT CHANGE −18 g, and an unrequested USER CONFIRMED appeared. The single label that survived verbatim is the one the entire safety rule depends on. So the model defended the constraint and improvised everything around it — check the semantics of any value it carries between frames, because it will keep the digits and swap the noun.
steps.prompt: Editorial evidence-capture frame on warm paper. One halftone yoghurt cup crop at center, surrounded by six precise registration boxes drawn in near-black ink: PRODUCT, USE BY, OPENED, STORAGE, QTY, and a final neutral box reading 'NO SAFETY VERDICT'. Boxes have thin rule lines, corner ticks, small tabular metadata labels, OCR-style alignment marks. Dry scanner aesthetic, condensed grotesk labels, cobalt accent #1755A5 for active registration. 16:9, 1920x1080. No glossy UI, no holograms, no scan beams, no people.
steps.result_label: 0:04.6 and 0:08.4 side by side · 18 JUN is USE BY, then PACKAGE DATE
steps.result_caption: Left: the invented dates 14 / 18 / 21 JUN. Right: the same 18 JUN relabelled PACKAGE DATE above an OPENED DATE of 14 JUN.

steps.title: The voiceover in the brief is not in the file
steps.text: The animation note for this reel promises a calm English voiceover explaining the logic in three sentences. Open the audio and it is not there. Twelve digital-silence gaps carve up 3.73 of the 19.09 seconds — 19.5% of the track is nothing at all — and the longest unbroken audible stretch is 2.65 seconds, ending at 0:10.49. Run a voicing test across the whole file and the longest continuously periodic run is 0.60 seconds; a spoken sentence needs several seconds of that back to back. What you are hearing is paper foley and stamp hits with hard gaps between them, which is a better soundtrack than the one described, but the brief and the file disagree and only one of them is real. Two more numbers worth correcting. The reel is 19.09 seconds over 458 frames at 24 fps, not the 20 seconds it is named after, and it goes completely static at 0:16.42 — the final lockup holds for 2.67 seconds without a single measurable change. There are also no hard cuts anywhere: the highest scene-change score in the entire file is 0.174, so the six keyframes dissolve into each other rather than cutting. And the watermark, briefed at 10% frame width flush to the bottom edge, measures 144 × 23 px — 7.5% of a 1920px frame, horizontally centred to within 1.5 px, sitting 13 px above the bottom.
steps.result_label: The delivered 19.09s reel · listen for the voiceover that was specified
steps.result_caption: 19.5% of the audio is digital silence. Longest audible stretch 2.65s, longest voiced run 0.60s. No cut scores above 0.174 in the whole file.

guides.result: A 19.09-second motion identity that keeps the promise it was built around and breaks several it made in passing. The safety rule holds frame for frame; the dates contradict themselves, the box labels rewrote themselves, and the voiceover was never recorded. Worth knowing which failures matter: none of these touch the constraint the project existed to protect.

guides.title: The plans hold to the millimetre. The labels on them do not.
guides.desc: Nine drawings of one converted factory, measured against each other in pixels. The survey grid comes back dimensionally perfect — 23.333 px/m on both axes, zero anisotropy, bay spacings with a standard deviation of 0.00 px — and the intervention sheet inherits it line for line. Then the annotations start describing a different building: a one-bay demolition note over a four-bay hole, a 2.0 m gallery drawn 0.85 m wide, and a section stretched 1.94× vertically while insisting all its floors are 4.50 m apart.

steps.title: The grid is exact, and the second sheet inherits it untouched
steps.text: This is the part that works, and it is worth more than it looks. Locate every column dot on the survey sheet and the four long bays measure 210.0, 210.0, 210.0, 210.0 px — standard deviation 0.00 — while the two short bays measure 140.0 and 140.0. That is 23.333 px/m in X and 23.333 px/m in Y: 0.00% anisotropy, so a circle drawn on this plan is a circle. Scan the perimeter and the wall centrelines sit 54.00 m apart the long way and 24.00 m the short way, exactly as briefed. Then generate the intervention diagram as a separate image and the grid does not move: identical column positions, identical y-lines at 439.5 / 579.5 / 719.5, identical building box. One column is gone, at grid 4/C, which is the single removal the prompt asked for. The bronze frame drawn around the void measures 420 × 280 px centreline to centreline = 18.00 × 12.00 m, matching the CONTROL dimension printed beside it. Two separately generated architectural sheets that agree with each other to the pixel — treat this as the baseline the rest of the set fails to reach.
steps.prompt: Create a concept-level measured as-built plan for a fictional 1912 textile factory. Footprint: 54.0 m × 24.0 m. Grid: 6 bays at 9.0 m in the long direction and 4 bays at 6.0 m in the short direction. Keep the brick perimeter, every cast-iron column, and two existing stairs in opposite corners. Draw as a precise architectural survey sheet, not a mood board. Include grid labels 1–7 and A–E, a north arrow, dimensions, and a 1:200 scale bar.

steps.result_caption: 23.333 px/m on both axes. Perimeter 54.00 × 24.00 m. The intervention sheet reproduces every one of these positions.

steps.title: Three labels that describe a different building
steps.text: The geometry is right and the writing on top of it is not. Three cases, all measured on the sheets themselves. First, the demolition note. The prompt said remove over bays 3–4 / B–C, the legend on the sheet repeats it, and the hole actually drawn spans gridlines 3 to 5 and B to D — four bays, not one — while the CONTROL dimension a few centimetres away correctly reads 18.0 × 12.0 m. The drawing and its own caption disagree in the same image. Second, the gallery. The upper-floor plan prints 2.0 m GALLERY ALL AROUND inside the void; the green band measures 22 px, and at that sheet's 25.833 px/m that is 0.85 m. Measure generously, from the inner face of the bronze frame to the void edge, and you still only get 1.35 m. Nobody walks a 0.85 m hotel gallery. Third, the key count. 20 keys per floor is four empty rectangles with captions on them. The two labelled 10 NORTH ROOMS and 10 SOUTH ROOMS measure 400 × 105 px = 15.48 × 4.07 m, so ten rooms inside one of them is 6.3 m² each, and not one partition, door or bathroom is drawn. The other two boxes read HOUSEKEEPING + ROOMS and ROOMS / SUITE AT END, which means the floor's real key count cannot be derived from the drawing at all. The pattern: the model is reliable at reproducing coordinates and unreliable at describing them. Trust its geometry, re-derive every number in its text.
steps.prompt: Create a typical upper-floor plan for levels +4.50 and +9.00 using the exact same 54 × 24 m grid and 18 × 12 m atrium void. Place 20 keys on each floor: 10 north-facing rooms, 10 south-facing rooms, with housekeeping and one suite at the east end. Keep the two existing stairs. Add a 2.0 m gallery all around the void. No room, bathroom or service enclosure may enter the atrium. Show level labels, grid, gallery width and room count.

steps.title: The one drawing whose job is proof is the one that is not to scale
steps.text: The section exists to verify that the lantern, galleries and retained roof coexist. It cannot, because it is not drawn to a single scale. Horizontally, the outer wall centrelines sit 1390 px apart for a building known to be 54.0 m long: 25.741 px/m. Vertically, the floor lines at +0.00, +4.50 and +9.00 sit exactly 225.0 px apart: 50.0 px/m. That is a 1.94× vertical stretch, so every angle, every roof pitch and the lantern's proportions on this sheet are fiction. Worse, the stretch is not even consistent within the drawing: the top storey, eaves down to +9.00, measures 120.0 px where the two below measure 225.0 px each — 53% of the height, while the labels insist on a uniform 4.50 m rhythm. Take the drawing at its own vertical scale and the eaves marked +13.50 sit 570 px above ground = 11.40 m. The atrium void, captioned 18 m ATRIUM VOID in the model's own type, measures 420 px = 16.32 m at the section's horizontal scale. The final render, linked at the end of this guide, was generated last and is the most persuasive image in the set; it shows two galleries above the ground floor, which is what the section draws — so the render is coordinated even though the drawing that was supposed to prove it is not. Read that as the lesson: photorealism arrived intact and orthographic discipline did not, and only one of those two is checkable by eye.
steps.prompt: Draw a longitudinal architectural section through the centre of the atrium. Show ground +0.00, level 1 +4.50, level 2 +9.00 and eaves +13.50. Retain the sawtooth roof outside the atrium. Cut the roof over the 18 m void and add a low-iron glass lantern set back 1.5 m from its edges. Show an independent dark bronze frame carrying the new lantern and gallery loads. Keep the existing brick shell separate from new steel. Add a concept-only engineering note that licensed structural and fire review is required.
steps.result_label: The delivered section · 25.741 px/m across, 50.0 px/m up

guides.result: Nine sheets in which the coordinates are trustworthy and the annotations are not. The survey and intervention grid are exact to 0.00 px and the render matches the section's storey count — but a one-bay note sits over a four-bay hole, the 2.0 m gallery is 0.85 m, and the section is stretched 1.94× vertically with one storey at half height. Concept study only; site survey and licensed structural, fire, access, MEP and conservation review are required before construction.
