guides.title: 4 of 5 silhouettes obeyed the brief — the 5th drew a different logo
guides.desc: One material formula, five brand silhouettes: YouTube, X, ChatGPT and Apple all rendered as briefed. The Quadcode slot didn't — asked for a four-pointed sparkle, it delivered Quadcode's own nested-square "Q" mark instead, with the stated gradient never happening either.

steps.title: 1. Lock the material formula once — then only swap the silhouette
steps.text: The series works because every icon shares one physical recipe: an inflated glossy-metal body, jewel/crystal accents, a pure black studio background and controlled rim lighting. Write that recipe as a fixed block and reuse it verbatim in all five prompts — the only variables are the brand silhouette and its signature color. Icon 01 tests the formula on the YouTube play button: a rounded red jeweled slab with the triangle read as a cut gem.
steps.prompt: Premium 3D brand icon, square 1:1, luxury product photography on a pure black studio background. Subject: the YouTube play-button icon reimagined as a physical jeweled object — a rounded-square slab of glossy inflated red metal, surface like polished automotive lacquer, with the white play triangle inset as a faceted crystal gem catching the light. Fine details: soft balloon-like inflation of the edges, crisp specular highlights, subtle red light bloom on the black floor, micro-scratches absent, showroom-clean. Lighting: one key light from upper left, cool rim light from the right, controlled reflections. Tangible and physical, NOT flat vector art, NOT a UI screenshot. Hard constraints: single object centered, generous negative space, no text, no watermark, no extra logos.

steps.title: 2. X — let black-on-black carry the drama
steps.text: The hardest slide: a black object on a black background. The trick is to spell out the separation mechanism — rim light and crystal facets do all the work. Describe the mark as cut obsidian with jeweled edges so the silhouette reads purely through highlights, not through color contrast.
steps.prompt: Premium 3D brand icon, square 1:1, luxury product photography on a pure black studio background. Subject: the X (Twitter) logomark reimagined as a physical jeweled object — a bold glossy black obsidian X with beveled crystal-cut edges, like a gem carved from dark glass, faint smoky depth inside the material. Separation from the background comes entirely from bright white rim lighting tracing every edge and sharp specular sparkles on the facets. Fine details: inflated rounded body, mirror-grade polish, subtle cool reflection pooled beneath the object. Tangible and physical, NOT flat vector art. Hard constraints: single object centered, generous negative space, no text, no watermark, no extra logos.

steps.title: 3. Quadcode — the model swapped the subject for its own logo
steps.text: The prompt asks for a four-pointed sparkle/star. What renders is Quadcode's actual nested-square "Q" bumper mark — no points, no apex where four points meet, so the promised "crystal core glowing at the center" has nothing to sit in; it's just a small flat coral square. The gradient fails too: sampling the top and base of the object gives #E86F5C and #F69892 — a 31-unit and 124-unit miss on the two target hexes, and the base reads lighter than the top, the opposite direction of "coral-to-crimson". Read as: when a brand name appears in the same sentence as its own logo, the model can substitute the logo for the described shape. State the geometry only ("four-pointed star, no lettering, no brand marks") if the sparkle is what you actually want.
steps.prompt: Premium 3D brand icon, square 1:1, luxury product photography on a pure black studio background. Subject: a four-pointed sparkle/star mark reimagined as a physical jeweled object — glossy inflated metal with a coral-to-crimson gradient finish flowing from #FF9569 at the top points to #DD344D at the base, like anodized liquid metal. A small crystal core glows softly at the center where the four points meet. Fine details: balloon-smooth inflation, razor-clean point tips, warm coral light spill on the black floor, restrained bloom. Lighting: warm key light, cool rim accents. Tangible and physical, NOT flat vector art. Hard constraints: single object centered, generous negative space, no text, no watermark, no extra logos.

steps.title: 4. ChatGPT knot — sell the geometry, not the gloss
steps.text: The knot's interlaced geometry is the whole recognition value, so the prompt protects it explicitly: 'keep every strand separate and readable'. Green gets stated as a material (jade-like metal), not a lighting gel — otherwise the model floods the whole frame green and kills the black background.
steps.prompt: Premium 3D brand icon, square 1:1, luxury product photography on a pure black studio background. Subject: the interlaced hexagonal knot mark reimagined as a physical jeweled object — six interwoven rounded strands of glossy jade-green metal, each strand inflated and balloon-smooth, weaving over and under each other with every strand separate and readable. Crystal-like highlights run along the strand curves; the weave casts soft internal shadows on itself. Fine details: showroom polish, faint green reflection beneath the object, background stays pure black. Lighting: key light from above, thin white rim light tracing the outer strands. Tangible and physical, NOT flat vector art. Hard constraints: single object centered, generous negative space, no text, no watermark, no extra logos.

steps.title: 5. Apple — asked for restraint, got the same stud count
steps.text: The prompt asks for "fewer sparkles than a gem" to close the set on a quieter note. Counting the diamonds on the render: about 10 studs ringing the apple body plus 2 on the leaf — the same density as the YouTube, X and ChatGPT icons before it, not a reduction. The brushed-silver material and separate polished leaf both land correctly; the "restraint" instruction is the one clause that didn't do anything. Then assemble all five into one 16:10 promo banner — feed the five finished icons back into GPT-Image as references and ask for a single editorial arrangement (that's exactly how the cover of this guide was made).
steps.prompt: Premium 3D brand icon, square 1:1, luxury product photography on a pure black studio background. Subject: the Apple logomark reimagined as a physical jeweled object — glossy inflated silver metal with a soft brushed-chrome finish, the leaf as a separate polished piece with a faint crystal edge. Understated elegance: fewer sparkles than a gem, more mirror-like surface perfection, cool neutral reflections. Fine details: balloon-smooth inflation, immaculate surface, subtle silver glow pooled on the black floor. Lighting: soft key light, crisp white rim light on the silhouette. Tangible and physical, NOT flat vector art. Hard constraints: single object centered, generous negative space, no text, no watermark, no extra logos.

guides.result: Four of five silhouettes rendered exactly as briefed: YouTube's play triangle read as a cut gem, X separated from a true black background through rim light alone, the ChatGPT knot kept all six strands distinct, Apple's leaf split into its own polished piece. The Quadcode slot is the exception on two counts — it drew the brand's own "Q" logo instead of the requested four-pointed sparkle, and its gradient never left flat coral. The other lesson came from Apple: telling the model to be "restrained" with sparkle density didn't reduce the stud count at all. Same reusable formula, same black studio — but silhouette and material instructions aren't guaranteed just because the surrounding recipe is fixed.

guides.title: Direct an epic boss-reveal cinematic shot
guides.desc: One warrior, one colossal tree-golem, a single glowing slash — build a AAA game-trailer beat in 15 seconds flat.

steps.title: 1. Design a boss silhouette you've never seen before
steps.text: Skip generic dragons. A living, cracked tree given a rough humanoid stance instantly reads as ancient and hostile without a single line of backstory — the cherry blossoms softening a threat make it feel like a cursed god of the forest, not a monster-of-the-week. Root-legs, molten-orange chest cracks, blossom-heavy branches and human-scale comparison all land as described. The one word that undersells its own result is "faint": the carved face isn't a subtle hint buried in bark, it's a fully legible skull with two glowing red-orange eyes sitting right above the chest crack — the single most eye-catching detail in the frame, not a background texture.
steps.prompt: A colossal ancient tree given a hulking humanoid silhouette — thick root-legs planted wide, gnarled bark skin split by glowing molten-orange cracks across its chest, branches heavy with pink cherry blossoms, a faint carved face buried in its trunk. Towering scale against a small human figure below. Cinematic realism, volumetric god-rays through blossom petals, dust and pollen drifting in the air, epic AAA game-trailer lighting.
steps.result_caption: The boss silhouette in full — including a carved face with two glowing eyes that reads far more "faint" in the prompt than it does on screen.

steps.title: 2. Block the shot like a director, not a slideshow — "no cuts" is the one instruction it dropped
steps.text: The armor, foreground petals and warm backlight are all there, and the wide-to-close blocking idea is sound in principle. But "no cuts" and "slow creeping push-in" don't survive: at 2.875s the shot hard-cuts (scene-detect score 0.53, more than 5x the noise floor of the rest of the clip) straight from the wide establishing frame to an extreme close-up on the warrior's gloved hand gripping the sword hilt — a jump cut, not a push-in. It's a good cut, dramatically, but it's the exact thing this step's own prompt explicitly banned.
steps.prompt: Cinematic single continuous shot, low wide-angle framing a giant tree-golem boss against cherry blossom trees and a misty stream, warrior in white lamellar armor with twin swords standing small in the foreground. Slow creeping push-in toward the confrontation, natural handheld micro-shake, warm late-afternoon backlight, shallow depth on foreground petals, 15 seconds, no cuts.
steps.result_caption: This excerpt starts just after the hard cut at 2.875s — the wide boss shot and this close-up on the hilt are two separate takes, not one continuous push-in.

steps.title: 3. Give the impact one clear VFX signature — the effect held, the "steady camera" didn't
steps.text: The VFX instruction is the one clean win in this whole sequence: there's exactly one golden energy arc, it reads clearly against the dark bark, and it's the only bright accent in the frame — no competing particle systems. "Camera holds steady through the impact" is the part that doesn't match: sampled every second from 5s to 9s, each frame is a genuinely different composition — low silhouette, tight shoulder shot, wide sweeping arc, a completely different angle on the chest fissure — which reads as a rapid sequence of whip-pans and reframes, not a held shot. It's not a second hard cut by the numbers (every reading in that window stays under the 0.3 cut threshold), but it's the opposite of steady.
steps.prompt: The warrior lunges and slashes upward with a katana, leaving one bright golden energy arc trailing the blade that cracks against the tree-golem's molten chest fissure, sparks and bark fragments scattering, camera holds steady through the impact, cherry blossom petals knocked loose drifting past frame, warm rim light, no text, no logos.
steps.result_caption: The impact signature is genuinely one clean golden arc. The camera around it, though, reframes completely from one second to the next rather than holding steady.

steps.title: 4. Cut it, don't trim it
steps.text: Rendered clips run long and often drift in the last second or two — pick the exact in/out points where the wind-up starts and the impact settles, instead of publishing the raw output. Press play above for the final 15-second cut.

guides.result: A striking boss design and a genuinely clean single VFX signature carry the piece. "One directed camera move" and "no cuts" oversell it, though: there's one real hard cut at 2.875s (wide shot straight to a hilt close-up) and the impact sequence at 5–9s is a rapid string of whip-pans and reframes rather than a held shot — closer to a fast-cut trailer than the single continuous take the brief called for.

guides.title: Retouch and color grade a product photo into a full ad set
guides.desc: Take one raw headphone photo and turn it into a commercial hero, a clean e-comm shot and a vertical detail — without killing the metal and leather textures.

steps.title: 1. Shoot (or generate) an honest raw source
steps.text: The whole exercise starts from a photo with real-world flaws — flat lighting, fingerprints and fine scratches on the metal, slight wear on the leather. Do not start from a perfect render; you need something to actually retouch. Keep materials detailed and lighting soft so you have room to push the grade later.
steps.prompt: Photorealistic product photograph of premium over-ear headphones on a clean dark studio background. Silver metal ear cups with visible fine scratches, smudges and fingerprints. Black leather ear cushions with natural texture and slight wear. Soft even studio lighting, no dramatic shadows, slightly flat color. Shot on 85mm lens, eye-level, centered composition, clean but imperfect — ready for retouch. High detail on materials, realistic reflections, no text, no logos, no watermark.

steps.title: 2. Retouch and grade the commercial hero
steps.text: This is the controlled edit — not a redesign. You remove scratches and smudges from the metal but keep it brushed and real (no plastic gloss, no chrome mirror). The leather keeps every bit of its grain; you clean dust, not texture. Then you re-light it into a premium hero and apply the cinematic grade. Reframe to 16:9 with breathing room on one side for a future headline.
steps.prompt: Retouch and re-light this exact headphone product photo into a premium commercial hero shot. Keep the same headphones, same materials, same identity — controlled edit only, no redesign. Retouch pass: remove fine scratches, smudges and fingerprints from the silver metal ear cups and yokes. Keep the metal brushed and real — no plastic gloss, no chrome mirror look. Preserve the leather grain on the headband and ear cushions exactly; clean only dust, not texture. Lighting and grade: dramatic premium studio lighting, large soft key from upper-left, cool rim light tracing the metal edges, deep charcoal background with a subtle warm gradient falloff. Rich cinematic color grade: deep blacks, lifted metal highlights, slightly warm silver tone, controlled reflections on the cups — elegant streaks, not chaos. Composition: reframe to a wide 16:9 hero crop, headphones slightly right of center with breathing room on the left for future headline text. Shot on 85mm, shallow depth of field, tack-sharp ear cups. No text, no logos, no watermark, no extra objects, no CGI plastic look.

steps.title: 3. Cut the clean e-comm catalog shot
steps.text: Same retouch rules, totally different light. Marketplaces need honesty: bright even lighting, a neutral seamless background, true-to-life color and the product centered and symmetrical. No stylized grade here — the goal is an accurate, trustworthy listing photo, not a mood piece.
steps.prompt: Retouch this exact headphone product photo into a clean e-commerce catalog shot. Same headphones, same materials, same identity — controlled edit only, no redesign. Retouch pass: remove fine scratches, smudges and fingerprints from the silver metal ear cups and yokes. Keep the metal brushed and real. Preserve leather grain on headband and ear cushions; clean only dust. Lighting and grade: bright, even, neutral catalog lighting — large soft frontal key, gentle fill, no harsh shadows, clean light-grey seamless background (#EDEDED). True-to-life color, no stylized grade: natural silver, deep natural black leather, balanced contrast for marketplaces. Composition: perfectly centered 1:1 square, headphones upright and symmetrical, generous even margins on all sides, product fills ~70% of frame height. Sharp focus across the whole product (f/8 look). No text, no badges, no price tags, no logos, no watermark, no props.

steps.title: 4. Pull the vertical texture detail
steps.text: The 9:16 detail sells the materials. Go macro on the seam where brushed metal meets leather — that tactile contrast is the whole shot. Raking light makes the texture cast micro-shadows. Match the hero's grade so the set reads as one shoot. Texture is the hero here; protect it above everything.
steps.prompt: Create a vertical macro detail shot from this exact headphone product photo. Same headphones, same materials — controlled edit only, no redesign. Subject: extreme close-up of one ear cup where the brushed silver metal meets the black leather cushion — the yoke hinge, the metal ring edge and the leather grain in one frame. Retouch pass: remove scratches, smudges and fingerprints from the metal. Keep the brushed texture and machining lines visible. Preserve leather grain exactly — every pore readable, no smoothing. Lighting and grade: moody macro lighting, raking key light skimming across the metal surface so texture casts micro-shadows, soft fill in the leather, deep dark background falling to black. Rich cinematic grade matching the hero shot: deep blacks, warm-leaning silver highlights, controlled specular streak along the metal edge. Composition: vertical 9:16, macro lens (100mm), shallow depth of field with the metal-leather seam in razor focus. No text, no logos, no watermark, no CGI look, no plastic metal, no blurred-out leather texture.

steps.title: 5. Upscale the set — but check the actual output size before calling it 4K
steps.text: The rule is right even if the delivered numbers here aren't: only add resolution, never reinterpret. What SeedVR2 actually returned for this set tops out at 1920px on the long edge (the hero) and 1200px on the e-comm square — real, clean, texture-preserving resolution, but roughly half of true 4K (3840px), not 4K itself. The retouch and grade held up on inspection: raw-source's dust and fine metal marks are visibly gone in the hero and e-comm crops, the leather grain reads pore-by-pore in the 9:16 detail, and the e-comm background sampled at #F0F0F0 against a #EDEDED target. Don't take an upscaler's output size on faith — measure the file before you write "4K" anywhere near it.
steps.prompt: Upscale this product photo 2x. Preserve exactly: brushed silver metal texture, black leather grain, the lighting and the color grade. Only add real resolution and crisp micro-detail — do not change lighting, grade, composition or materials. Texture fidelity is everything; no smoothing, no hallucinated detail.

guides.result: A complete, coherent product set from one raw photo: a cinematic 16:9 hero, an honest 1:1 e-comm catalog shot and a vertical 9:16 texture detail — retouch, grade and neutral e-comm background all verified against the raw source. The one gap: the set was upscaled to 1920px, not the 3840px "4K" the last step promises — call it what it measures, not what the step title says.

guides.title: Four different briefs, one template — read the pattern before you trust it
guides.desc: Four business visuals — recurring revenue, AI onboarding, landing-page speed, a CRM fix — each prompt asks for a different structure. The model rendered all four as the same red-and-black "Before / After" split, and ignored two explicit bans along the way.

steps.title: 1. Show recurring revenue as a system — minus the ban it broke
steps.text: The prompt explicitly says "no fake statistics" and the render ignores it: a dashboard reading $124,560 revenue, +18.6%, $8,420 earnings, 23,689 visitors, 5.2% conversion, plus four floating "Payment received +$1,250 / +$2,340 / +$1,890 / +$980" cards — none of them real, all of them precise-looking. The mechanism itself does land: the right side visibly shows payment → service continuing → customer relaxing, which is the actual point of a recurring-revenue visual. Ban the specific thing you don't want ("no invented dollar or percentage figures"), not the vague category ("no fake statistics") — the model reads the second as decoration, not a rule.
steps.prompt: Create a clear premium business illustration explaining recurring revenue. Show a simple continuous loop between customer, payment and active service, with a readable 24/7 operating rhythm. Use a clean editorial SaaS style, strong hierarchy, restrained palette, real interface fragments rather than generic arrows, no fake statistics, no illegible microtext.

steps.title: 2. Contrast manual onboarding with AI onboarding
steps.text: The visual needs one contrast only: a slow hand-built process on one side, an automated flow on the other. People should understand the time saving before reading a caption.
steps.prompt: Create a split business visual comparing manual onboarding versus AI onboarding. Left: fragmented handoffs, repeated data entry, waiting and confusion. Right: one guided automated flow, instant setup and clear next steps. Professional editorial SaaS art direction, readable contrast, few elements, no decorative clutter, no fake logos.

steps.title: 3. Make a landing page's speed visible
steps.text: Do not render a generic browser mockup. Show the commercial consequence: a page that takes a week to ship versus a focused flow that gets the message and call-to-action live fast.
steps.prompt: Create a crisp business visual about shipping a landing page in one week. Show a focused sequence from brief to launch: message, page structure, build and live result. Make speed readable through progress and momentum, not flames or racing cars. Premium product-design editorial style, clear hierarchy, no fake analytics, no tiny unreadable text.

steps.title: 4. Replace spreadsheet chaos with a CRM view — but the ban list has a hole in it
steps.text: The pipeline itself is legitimately good: New Leads → Qualified → Proposal → Closed Won reads instantly, with a Pipeline Value and Conversion Rate card giving it weight. But the prompt's "no brand names" ban only got applied to the After side — the Before panel's sidebar renders an actual LinkedIn icon (the lower-case "in" mark) among its integration icons, a real trademarked logo the ban should have caught. If a ban needs to hold on both halves of a before/after, say so explicitly on both halves — a single blanket instruction at the end of the prompt is easy for the model to apply unevenly.
steps.prompt: Create a business before-and-after visual: an overloaded spreadsheet with duplicate customer rows, unclear ownership and missed follow-ups transforms into a clean CRM pipeline with visible stages, owner avatars and next actions. Product-led editorial design, strong information hierarchy, realistic but minimal interface detail, no brand names, no illegible text.

guides.result: Four business visuals that explain a real operational change in seconds. All four converged on the same red-and-black "Before / After" split composition — only one of the four prompts actually asked for a before/after, the other three just drifted there anyway. Two hard bans didn't hold: "no fake statistics" left a full dashboard of invented dollar figures in the revenue slide, and "no brand names" caught the After side of the CRM slide but missed a real LinkedIn icon sitting in the Before side. Useful output, but proofread every number and every icon before it ships.

guides.title: "Same room, three directions" — except it's three different rooms
guides.desc: The brief asks for one locked room compared across three material directions. What rendered is three unrelated spaces: a double-height barn hall with a spiral staircase, a single-story brick loft with no staircase, and a glass-walled high-rise apartment with a city skyline. Same idea, but the "identical room" claim doesn't survive a side-by-side look.

steps.title: 1. Lock what must stay the same — the model unlocked it anyway
steps.text: The instruction is exactly right: keep architecture, camera angle, daylight direction and proportions identical, vary only the material direction. Look at what actually rendered across the three: the Baroque version is a double-height barn hall with a spiral staircase and timber-beam vault; the industrial loft is a single-story brick space with no staircase or upper floor at all; the modern studio is a standard-ceiling high-rise apartment with a floor-to-ceiling city view. Three different buildings, three different ceiling heights, three different window walls — not one room in three finishes. If the room must be identical, generate the empty locked room ONCE as its own reference image first, then feed that exact image back into each direction prompt as an edit — don't describe the room in text three separate times and hope it converges.
steps.prompt: Create three high-end real-estate interior concepts for the exact same compact urban living room. Keep the architecture, camera angle, daylight direction and room proportions identical in every version. The comparison must show only the interior direction changing: furniture, material palette, lighting mood and decorative language. Editorial property-photography quality, realistic scale, no people, no text.

steps.title: 2. Push the Baroque cottage direction
steps.text: For a character-led property, use dark timber, aged brass, velvet and framed art. The goal is not random luxury props; it is a warm, layered room that sells atmosphere at first glance.
steps.prompt: Using the locked room brief, create the Baroque cottage direction: dark walnut joinery, muted olive walls, aged brass details, a deep plum velvet sofa, antique framed oil paintings, patterned wool rug, warm late-afternoon window light and restrained candle-like practical lamps. Rich but lived-in, high-end property editorial photography, no text.

steps.title: 3. Switch to an industrial loft
steps.text: For a sharper, city-facing listing, replace decoration with material contrast: concrete, black steel, reclaimed wood and one strong leather piece. Keep the room functional — buyers still need to see where they would sit, work and eat.
steps.prompt: Using the locked room brief, create the industrial loft direction: exposed concrete, black steel-framed glass, reclaimed oak, a cognac leather sofa, graphite textiles, sculptural pendant lights and clear daylight. Keep the space warm enough to live in, not like an empty warehouse. Premium real-estate editorial photography, no text.

steps.title: 4. Strip it back into a modern studio
steps.text: For the broadest buyer appeal, use a quiet palette and fewer objects. A modern studio succeeds when the layout reads instantly and every piece earns its place.
steps.prompt: Using the locked room brief, create the modern studio direction: warm white walls, pale oak, a modular cream sofa, brushed aluminium accents, one large abstract artwork, soft indirect lighting and discreet storage. Calm, spacious, design-led and practical. Premium real-estate editorial photography, no text.

guides.result: Three individually strong, coherent interior renders — but not a valid same-room comparison. Baroque cottage is a double-height barn hall, industrial loft is a single-story brick space, modern studio is a high-rise apartment: different ceiling heights, different window walls, no shared architecture between any of the three. Useful as three separate mood boards; not useful as evidence that one room "works" in three directions, because no single room was ever actually held constant.

guides.title: Upscale real product footage — but check what resolution you actually shipped
guides.desc: Turn a soft handheld watch shoot into a crisp before/after with one Topaz pass. The delivered master measures 1920×1080 — sharper, not 4K, despite the on-screen "AFTER 4K" label.

steps.title: Match the model to your footage
steps.text: Real product photography isn't heavily compressed or synthetic, so skip the specialty models and start with the general-purpose one — it sharpens detail without over-smoothing metal reflections and skin-tone gemstones into plastic.
steps.prompt:
UTILITY: topaz
VIDEO-INPUT: rolex-source.mp4
MODEL: Proteus
TARGET_FPS: 30
steps.result_caption: Dial macro, before and after. The model matched to this footage keeps engraving crisp without inventing texture.

steps.title: Keep the upscale factor and noise conservative — and do the math on where it lands you
steps.text: For footage that's already reasonably sharp, 2x beats 4x — pushing harder just amplifies grain instead of adding real detail. Keep noise and compression in the 0.1-0.3 range so the case metal and dial texture stay crisp. What this doesn't mention: a 2x factor only reaches true 4K (3840×2160) if your source is already 1920×1080. This render's final master is 1920×1080 total, split into two side-by-side halves — meaning the source going into this pass was well under 1080p, and 2x lands the output around standard HD, not 4K. The on-screen "AFTER 4K" label baked into every frame overstates the actual output by one full resolution tier.
steps.prompt:
UTILITY: topaz
VIDEO-INPUT: rolex-source.mp4
MODEL: Proteus
UPSCALE_FACTOR: 2
NOISE: 0.2
COMPRESSION: 0.2
H264_OUTPUT: true
steps.result_caption: Beach shot, cropped straight from the delivered master — which measures 1920×1080 despite the "AFTER 4K" caption printed on it.

steps.title: Render and cut the before/after
steps.text: Run the pass, then cut between the original and the upscaled clip on the same shot so the sharpness gain is obvious at a glance, not just claimed in a caption. That's the right instinct — which is exactly why it's worth noticing the on-screen caption in this render says something the pixels don't back up: "AFTER 4K" is printed on every frame of a video that measures 1920×1080 end to end. Play the clip above and judge the sharpness gain on its own; don't take the caption's resolution claim at face value.

guides.result: The sharpness gain from before to after is real and visible. The "4K" part of the pitch isn't: the delivered master is 1920×1080, and the "AFTER 4K" caption baked into the video overstates the output by one full resolution tier. Judge this as a solid HD upscale, not a 4K delivery.

guides.title: Pitch a flying ironing-drone concept ad
guides.desc: Turn a wild what-if into a punchy product-ad concept: a hovering drone that steam-irons your shirt mid-air.

steps.title: Invent the product in one line
steps.text: Name the object and the twist in a single sentence — a compact drone with a heated glide bar is a small enough leap to feel plausible, but strange enough to stop the scroll.
steps.prompt: A sleek white quadcopter drone about the size of a dinner plate hovers beside a hanging crisp white dress shirt on a wooden hanger, a thin heated glide bar mounted under its body gliding down the fabric like a flatiron, wisps of steam rising from the contact point, dark charcoal studio background, dramatic side lighting, moody premium product-ad photography, no text.
steps.result_caption: The product exists from frame one. The single-line invention is the whole brief.

steps.title: Direct the ironing pass and the captions
steps.text: Script it like a real spec ad: name each beat and give the exact caption text for each one, so the render stays on-message instead of drifting into generic footage.
steps.prompt: The drone glides slowly down each panel of the shirt, steam trailing behind its heated bar, wrinkles visibly smoothing wherever it passes. Cut between beats with these on-screen captions, small caps, bottom-center, clean sans-serif: "THIS IS IRONDRONE" then "GLIDING STEAM" then "LASER PRECISION" then "EVERY CREASE — ERASED, MID-AIR" then "CRUMPLED — TO FLAWLESS". End on the shirt hanging perfectly flat and crease-free. Same dark studio, same lighting throughout, no extra text.
steps.result_caption: The ironing pass with captions riding along. Both were directed in the same prompt.

steps.title: Generate and keep the cleanest pass — check both sleeves, not just the one the drone worked
steps.text: Steam reads as heat, not fog, and the near sleeve — the one the drone actually glides across — genuinely goes from crumpled to smooth by 5-6s. But the far sleeve (screen-left, on the side the drone never visits) is still visibly crumpled at 9.8s, one frame from the end of a 10.05s clip. "Crumpled — to flawless" is only true for half the shirt; the take that got kept has an un-ironed sleeve sitting right next to the perfectly pressed one it's supposed to demonstrate.
steps.result_caption: The near sleeve is smooth, but look at the far sleeve on the left — still crumpled here and still crumpled one frame before the clip ends.

guides.result: The strongest parts of this render are the parts nobody usually checks: all five on-screen captions match the prompt's exact wording, order and bottom-center placement, and the near sleeve genuinely goes from crumpled to smooth. The one miss is the payoff itself — the far sleeve is still visibly crumpled one frame before the clip ends, so "crumpled to flawless" only describes half the shirt.

guides.title: Museum of Impossible Things: a 5-image carousel with one prompt formula
guides.desc: Five physically impossible exhibits shot like real museum photography — a water knot, frozen lightning, fire inside ice, a storm in a bottle and a folded human shadow. One reusable scene formula, five swappable subjects, readable plaques on every frame.

steps.title: 1. Lock the scene formula once — then only swap the exhibit
steps.text: The whole series rides on one fixed skeleton: a pitch-dark museum hall with black velvet walls, one hard spotlight, a charcoal velvet pedestal, and a graphite plaque with a gradient accent strip. Every prompt starts with the same camera line — 'Award-winning museum exhibition photograph, square 1:1, medium-format Hasselblad, 80mm lens, extremely fine micro-detail' — and ends with the same bans: no CGI plastic look, no stock blandness, no extra text. The only thing that changes between the five images is the impossible object on the pedestal and the plaque text. That's what makes five separate generations read as one exhibition. Exhibit 01 tests the formula: a trefoil knot tied from flowing water, hovering above the velvet with caustic light patterns underneath.
steps.prompt: Award-winning museum exhibition photograph, square 1:1 composition, shot on medium-format Hasselblad, 80mm lens, razor-sharp focus on the exhibit, extremely fine micro-detail. Scene: a pitch-dark museum hall, walls of black velvet swallowing all light. One single hard spotlight beam cuts down through faint dust. Hero subject, filling most of the frame: a thick rope tied into a perfect trefoil knot — made entirely of living, flowing crystal-clear water. Visible surface tension skin, internal turbulence, strings of micro-bubbles racing through the loops, dozens of individual droplets frozen mid-orbit around the knot, each droplet acting as a tiny lens. The knot hovers above a round pedestal upholstered in deep charcoal velvet — velvet fiber texture clearly visible. Sharp bright caustic light patterns dance across the velvet under the knot. Color and light: deep glacial blue-white water against warm amber spill on the velvet, saturated punchy cinematic grade, crushed blacks, high dynamic range. Tangible and physical — a photograph of a real impossible object, NOT a 3D render, NOT smooth CGI plastic. In the lower portion of the frame: a museum plaque — matte graphite metal plate with a thin glowing gradient strip along its top edge running from coral orange (#FF9569) to crimson red (#DD344D). Plaque text painted white, upright regular sans-serif (NOT italic), perfectly sharp and legible, EXACTLY verbatim: "WATER KNOT" / "Exhibit No. 01 — Fluid Dynamics Hall" / "Tied once. Never untied. The water has been flowing through itself since the day it was knotted." Hard constraints: no cyberpunk, no neon, no sci-fi props, no people, no watermarks, no logos, no extra text, no plastic CGI look.

steps.title: 2. Frozen Lightning — make the impossible object the only light source
steps.text: The trick that sells this frame: the exhibit itself lights the scene. The bolt is described as white-hot plasma (not a purple neon tube — ban that explicitly, or you'll get a lamp), and physicality comes from consequences: a scorched blackened ring on the velvet where the bolt touches it, glowing embers at its rim, a wisp of smoke. If your plaque text comes out italic, add 'upright regular sans-serif (NOT italic)' — that one line fixed it here.
steps.prompt: Award-winning museum exhibition photograph, square 1:1 composition, shot on medium-format Hasselblad, 80mm lens, razor-sharp focus on the exhibit, extremely fine micro-detail. Scene: a pitch-dark museum hall, walls of black velvet swallowing all light. Hero subject, filling most of the frame: a real lightning bolt frozen solid mid-strike, displayed upright like a sculpture on a round pedestal upholstered in deep charcoal velvet (velvet fiber texture clearly visible). The bolt is a jagged branching column of blinding white-hot plasma, completely motionless — every filament crisp and separate, hair-thin secondary tendrils splitting off the main channel, dozens of tiny sparks suspended motionless in the air around it like insects trapped in amber. Where the bolt meets the velvet, the fabric is scorched into a delicate blackened ring with glowing orange embers at its rim, a thin wisp of smoke rising. Faint crackled glassy texture on the plasma surface, heat shimmer distortion in the air around it. Color and light: the bolt is the only light source — blinding white core with violet-blue falloff, hard shadows, crushed blacks, saturated punchy cinematic grade, high dynamic range. NOT a 3D render, NOT smooth CGI plastic, NOT a purple neon lamp. In the lower portion of the frame: a museum plaque — matte graphite metal plate with a thin glowing gradient strip along its top edge running from coral orange (#FF9569) to crimson red (#DD344D). Plaque text painted white, upright regular sans-serif (NOT italic), perfectly sharp and legible, EXACTLY verbatim: "FROZEN LIGHTNING" / "Exhibit No. 02 — Storm Preservation Wing" / "Captured 0.003 seconds before impact. Still warm. Do not tap the glass." Hard constraints: no cyberpunk, no neon city, no sci-fi props, no people, no watermarks, no logos, no extra text.

steps.title: 3. Ice with Fire — the color-clash hero of the series
steps.text: This is the loudest slide, built on one violent contrast: blazing orange fire core versus glacial blue-cyan ice shell. Push both to maximum saturation and let the fire light travel through internal fractures so every crack becomes a glowing amber vein. Physicality anchors that keep it from looking CGI: frost bloom, cold droplets sweating down the faces, trapped air bubbles in ancient ice layers, and a glassy refrozen rim of meltwater on the velvet below.

Deep inside the crystal-clear ice a real campfire burns — sharp orange-gold flames with visible flame licks, glowing red embers and charred logs at its base, all fully sealed within the ice. The fire light travels through internal fractures, turning every crack into a glowing amber vein across the block. The ice exterior is hyper-detailed: frost bloom, sweating cold droplets running down the faces, tiny trapped air bubbles in ancient layers, razor-sharp chipped edges. Thin freezing mist rolls off the block and pools around the pedestal base. Below the block, melted water refreezes into a glassy rim on the velvet. Color and light: violent clash — blazing orange fire core versus deep glacial blue-cyan ice shell, saturated punchy cinematic grade, crushed blacks, high dynamic range. NOT a 3D render, NOT smooth CGI plastic. In the lower portion of the frame: a museum plaque — matte graphite metal plate with a thin glowing gradient strip along its top edge running from coral orange (#FF9569) to crimson red (#DD344D). Plaque text painted white, upright regular sans-serif (NOT italic), perfectly sharp and legible, EXACTLY verbatim: "ICE WITH FIRE" / "Exhibit No. 03 — Thermodynamics Denial Hall" / "The fire refuses to melt it. The ice refuses to put it out. They have agreed to disagree." Hard constraints: no cyberpunk, no neon, no sci-fi props, no people, no watermarks, no logos, no extra text.

steps.title: 4. Storm in a Bottle — change the scale, keep the system
steps.text: Four monumental exhibits in a row get monotonous. Slide four drops to macro scale: a 40 cm antique bottle with a full thunderstorm inside. Ask for 'macro-level sharpness' instead of the standard focus line and load the prompt with tiny believable details — condensation streaks inside the glass, bubbles in the hand-blown glass itself, cracking wax on the cork, one wisp of cloud escaping the seal. The internal lightning flash does the lighting job again, carving the bottle silhouette out of the darkness.

steps.title: 5. Folded Human Shadow — close on the concept, not the spectacle
steps.text: The finale trades fireworks for a paradox: a human shadow folded like boutique silk, lying inside a bright spotlight yet staying absolute black. The prompt spells the contradiction out — 'it lies directly inside the bright spotlight yet remains total, light-devouring black, zero reflection'. Recognizability sells it: a face profile on the top layer, a folded arm, shadow fingers hanging over the edge. Two extra touches give it life: one corner curling up as if about to unfold, and the velvet subtly darker around the stack, as if the shadow stains what it touches. Plaque copy carries the storytelling — write it like a real museum label with one unsettling line.
steps.prompt: Award-winning museum exhibition photograph, square 1:1 composition, shot on medium-format Hasselblad, 80mm lens, razor-sharp focus on the exhibit, extremely fine micro-detail. Scene: a pitch-dark museum hall, walls of black velvet swallowing all light. One single hard warm spotlight beam from above with faint dust drifting through it. Hero subject, filling most of the frame: a full-size human shadow — a flat, absolutely black silhouette of a standing person — carefully folded like fine silk fabric into a neat boutique-style stack, displayed on a round pedestal upholstered in deep charcoal velvet (velvet fiber texture clearly visible). The folded stack is instantly readable: the profile of a face on the top layer, a folded arm tucked into the second layer, slender shadow fingers spilling over the edge of the fold and hanging in the air. The shadow material is impossible: it lies directly inside the bright spotlight yet remains total, light-devouring black — zero reflection, deeper black than anything else in the frame. Its edges are soft and feathered exactly like a real cast shadow, yet it holds crisp fabric creases; one corner curls up slightly as if the shadow is about to unfold itself. Around the stack the velvet is subtly darker, as if the shadow slowly stains what it touches. Color and light: warm amber spotlight against charcoal darkness, the folded shadow reading as an absolute black hole in the image, saturated punchy cinematic grade, crushed blacks, high dynamic range. guides.result: A five-image carousel that reads as one exhibition: same hall, same velvet pedestal, same branded plaque system (graphite plate, coral-to-crimson gradient strip, readable sans-serif labels) — with five different impossible objects. All frames generated square 2880x2880 in GPT-Image, no upscaling needed. Reuse the formula: keep the scene skeleton, swap the exhibit, rewrite the plaque.

guides.title: Boss fight: one brief, two AI models
guides.desc: Give the same boss-fight brief to two video models and cut the takes side by side — the split-screen format that starts arguments in the comments.

steps.title: Write one brief both models get
steps.text: The comparison only works if the brief is identical. Describe the fight beats — approach, dodge, counter — but leave the world open, so each model shows its own taste in setting and monster design.
steps.prompt: Cinematic dark-fantasy boss fight, game-cinematic quality: a lone armored hero faces a towering monstrous boss, the hero approaches weapon drawn, dodges a massive strike, and counters. Dynamic camera following the action, dramatic lighting, volumetric atmosphere, photoreal detail, 18 seconds
steps.result_caption: Both models, first frame, same brief. Any difference from here on is the model's decision.

steps.title: Generate a take on each model
steps.text: Run the exact same prompt on both models. In this run one staged a plague abomination in a flooded gothic cathedral, the other a horned demon in a torch-lit colosseum — same beats, totally different directors.
steps.result_caption: The same beat on each model, side by side. One take each, no reroll.

steps.title: Cut the split-screen with labels
steps.text: Place the takes side by side, label each half with the model name, and let them run in sync. Viewers pick a winner themselves — that's the engagement hook. Play the clip above to see the result.

guides.title: Shoot a movie-grade mutation VFX scene
guides.desc: A syringe of glowing serum, a burst of pink energy, and a crystalline monster towering over fleeing scientists — one continuous lab-horror shot.

steps.title: Open on a macro detail
steps.text: Start tight and quiet: a needle piercing a specimen fills the frame. A macro close-up buys believability before the chaos — viewers lean in before the scene turns.
steps.prompt: Extreme macro close-up in a research lab: a syringe filled with glowing neon-pink serum slowly injects into a small yellow gelatinous specimen on a teal lab table, clinical lighting, shallow depth of field, cinematic film look
steps.result_caption: The macro opener: needle in the yolk. Scale is established before anything moves.

steps.title: Detonate the transformation
steps.text: Describe the energy burst as a physical event — light, particles, shockwave shaking the room. The camera should get 'hit' by it too: motion blur and grain sell that something went very wrong.
steps.prompt: The specimen erupts in a blinding surge of pink energy, particles and plasma flooding the laboratory, equipment silhouetted against the blast, handheld camera shaken by the shockwave, heavy motion blur and film grain, VFX-heavy cinematic sequence
steps.result_caption: The detonation. It is one continuous transformation, not a cut to an after-state.

steps.title: Reveal the creature
steps.text: End wide: the monster standing in the wrecked lab while people run. Naming 'scientists fleeing in panic' gives the creature scale and turns a VFX test into a movie scene. Play the clip above to see the result.
steps.prompt: A towering crystalline monster with glowing pink translucent skin stands in the wrecked laboratory, smoke and pink mist around it, scientists in lab coats fleeing in panic, wide cinematic shot, dramatic overhead lighting, photoreal creature VFX

guides.result: A 10-second lab-horror VFX sequence — macro injection, energy blast, creature reveal — that reads like a blockbuster teaser.

guides.title: Drowned king colossus: two models, one legend
guides.desc: A viking longship meets a crowned colossus rising from the sea — the same epic prompt rendered by two AI models, cut into one split-screen.

steps.title: Script the scene in three beats
steps.text: Big prompts fall apart without structure. Lock three beats — the colossus looms over the ship, the ship capsizes underwater, an extreme close-up of the giant's eye — and both models have to hit the same marks.
steps.prompt: Epic dark-fantasy sequence in three beats: 1) a viking longship with shields and torn sail sails toward a colossal drowned king — a mountain-sized ancient giant with a crown, seaweed beard and waterfalls pouring off his stone-like skin, storm sky; 2) underwater shot of the capsized longship sinking, vikings and shields drifting down in green murky water; 3) extreme close-up of the colossus' enormous pale eye opening underwater. Cinematic photoreal detail, 18 seconds
steps.result_caption: Beat one of three: surface, ship, king. The script gave both models the same three beats.

steps.title: Run it on both models
steps.text: Same prompt, two models, no cherry-picking edits inside a take. The differences you keep — crown design, water physics, how the eye opens — are exactly what makes the comparison worth watching.
steps.result_caption: Beat two underwater on both models. Same words, visibly different readings.

steps.title: Sync the halves and label them
steps.text: Line both takes up beat-for-beat in a split-screen and put the model names on top. Matching beats side by side is what makes quality differences impossible to miss. Play the clip above to see the result.

guides.result: An 18-second split-screen epic where two AI models raise the same drowned king from the sea — beat-synced so the differences do the talking.

guides.title: Fake a viral walking-on-water clip
guides.desc: A woman steps off the pier and runs across the ocean while the crowd films — the impossible moment that floods comment sections.

steps.title: Stage it like real phone footage
steps.text: The trick is the witnesses. Put a crowd with phones on the pier — if bystanders are filming, viewers' brains read the clip as documentary, not CGI.
steps.prompt: Handheld phone footage at a tropical resort pier, a crowd of tourists in swimwear stands on the wooden dock filming with their phones, crystal-clear turquoise lagoon, a small boat anchored in the distance, bright midday sun, candid vertical-video energy, realistic colors, no cinematic grading
steps.result_caption: A crowd holding phones, a pier, midday sun. The staging says "someone filmed this", not "a studio lit this".

steps.title: Direct the impossible moment
steps.text: Describe one continuous action with real physics: she steps off the pier onto the water and runs. Name the splashes and the foam trail — believable water reaction is what sells the fake.
steps.prompt: A young woman in a white crop top and black shorts steps off the pier directly onto the ocean surface and walks on the water, then breaks into a run across the lagoon toward the beach, her feet slap the surface leaving splashes and a long white foam trail behind her, the crowd on the pier keeps filming in disbelief, camera follows her from behind, natural body mechanics, realistic water physics, 11 seconds
steps.result_caption: The impossible step off the pier. The camera keeps its phone-footage wobble through it.

steps.title: Keep the take that fools people
steps.text: Generate a few takes and keep the one where the feet actually read as striking the surface — one bad footstep breaks the whole illusion. Play the clip above to see the result.

guides.title: A jazz R&B restaurant track that cannot loop in a restaurant
guides.desc: One prompt, 3:39 of smooth fine-dining lounge. The tempo instruction landed almost exactly — 85 BPM asked, 86.1 measured. Two things did not: it fades out to silence over the last twelve seconds, and it is mastered at −13 LUFS with the true peak sitting on 0.0 dBFS. Both are fixable, neither is obvious until you measure.

steps.title: Put the number in the prompt — it is the instruction that survives
steps.text: Mood words are negotiable, numbers are not. This prompt asked for "relaxed 85 BPM"; beat-tracking the finished file returns 86.1 BPM, and it holds that tempo from the first bar to the last. Everything vaguer got looser: "smooth dynamics" came back as a loudness range of 5.3 LU, which is narrower than the phrase suggests — the track barely breathes. Write the values you actually care about (tempo, key, length, no vocals) as numbers and words the model can only read one way, then let it improvise on the adjectives.
steps.prompt: Sophisticated jazz R&B instrumental for an upscale fine-dining restaurant lounge, smooth, elegant and relaxed. Warm Rhodes electric piano, soft brushed drums, walking upright bass, mellow muted trumpet and tenor saxophone, lush jazz chords. Relaxed 85 BPM, subtle vinyl warmth, tasteful and understated, no vocals
steps.result_caption: The opening twelve seconds. Tempo measured across the whole file: 86.1 BPM against the 85 that was asked for.

steps.title: The arrangement changes where the model decides, not where you expect
steps.text: A restaurant track lives or dies on where it moves. Measure that instead of guessing: track loudness and spectral centroid second by second and the real events show up as numbers. In this file the biggest arrangement change is at 2:01 — energy in the 2–5 kHz band, where a lead horn sits, drops from 20.8% to 10.2% of the spectrum while the low mids swell from 14.5% to 22.2%. The lead simply stops and the rhythm section takes the room back. Nothing comparable happens in the first minute: compare 0:10–0:22 with 0:40–0:52 and the centroid moves 1895 Hz → 1916 Hz, which is nothing. If you need a change at a specific minute, generate in sections and join them — one prompt gives you one shape and it is the model's shape.
steps.result_caption: The only structural move in three and a half minutes: the lead drops out at 2:01 and does not come back.

steps.title: Two numbers decide whether it works in a real room — and both are wrong here
steps.text: First: it fades. Over the final twelve seconds the level walks down −9, −9, −11, −11, −12, −12, −15, −16, −15, −16, −18, −24 dB into silence. A fade is the one ending that cannot loop, and background music is a loop by definition — every three minutes forty the room goes quiet and everybody notices. Second: the master is hot. Integrated loudness is −13 LUFS with the true peak resting on 0.0 dBFS, which is a mastering-for-Spotify number, not a dinner-service number; rooms want roughly −18 LUFS and a peak with headroom left in it. Neither needs a re-generation. Trim the last twelve seconds at the final downbeat, cross-fade the head over the tail for a seamless loop, then normalise the file to −18 LUFS with a −1 dBTP limiter. Two minutes of editing turns an unusable render into a usable one.
steps.result_label: The final twelve seconds, uncut and unedited · 3:27.8–3:39.8
steps.result_caption: No fades were added to this excerpt — the fade you hear is in the delivered file, dropping 15.2 dB into silence.

guides.result: 3:39.8 of convincing fine-dining jazz at 86.1 BPM — plus the two edits nobody tells you about: cut the fade so it can actually loop, and pull it from −13 to −18 LUFS so it can sit under conversation.

guides.title: Shoot a 2000s camcorder memory
guides.desc: Turn one prompt into a nostalgic MiniDV street clip that feels like real found footage.

steps.title: Pick the camera, not the style
steps.text: The trick is to describe the device that filmed it. Name a real 2000s camcorder look and the AI stops making glossy footage.
steps.prompt: Footage filmed on a 2004 MiniDV handycam with a fisheye lens attachment, slight barrel distortion, soft focus, washed-out colors, mild tape noise, white date-time stamp in the corner reading 2004. 5.29 AM 10:47, 4:3 home-video framing
steps.result_caption: Fisheye vignette, DV colour, burned-in date. The camera was specified, not the style.

steps.title: Direct one small, real moment
steps.text: Big scenes look fake on old tape. One quiet everyday moment sells the illusion — say exactly who does what.
steps.prompt: A quiet back alley in Seoul on a sunny morning, a young woman with a loose ponytail crouches on the cracked pavement and slowly reaches her open hand toward a stray tabby cat, the cat sniffs her fingers, old tires and a dark green metal gate behind them, candid handheld moment
steps.result_caption: The one small moment: a stray cat, a hand held out. Nothing else happens, and nothing else needs to.

steps.title: Generate and keep the honest take
steps.text: Run both parts as one prompt in Seedance, 15 seconds. Pick the take with natural motion — small pauses and imperfect framing are what make it believable. Play the clip above to see the result.
steps.result_caption: The glance back. This is the honest take — the one that was kept over prettier, stiffer ones.

guides.result: A 15-second retro camcorder clip that looks like a real memory from 2004 — ready for reels, moodboards or a music video.

guides.title: Mass-produce UGC ads from one product photo
guides.desc: Build an AI actor, hand them your product and generate ultra-realistic UGC ad clips on repeat.

steps.title: Create your AI actor
steps.text: Generate one consistent, believable creator with GPT-Image. Keep the look casual and trustworthy — this face will front all your ads.
steps.prompt: Photorealistic portrait of a female UGC creator in her early 30s, natural blonde hair, soft daylight, beige wool coat over a cream turtleneck, neutral warm background, looking at camera with a calm friendly expression, shot on a mirrorless camera, 85mm, realistic skin texture, no retouching look
steps.result_caption: The pipeline: actor → prompt → product → output. The actor tile is the same in every frame.

steps.title: Put the product in her hands
steps.text: Combine the actor and your product photo into one natural shot. Name the product and the action — the AI does the compositing.
steps.prompt: The same woman naturally holds and presents a black leather tote bag to the camera, fingers resting on the top edge of the bag, soft indoor daylight, candid UGC style, product clearly visible and in focus, realistic hands, no studio look
steps.result_caption: Bag in hand, consistent with the product tile. The compositing step is what puts it there.

steps.title: Bring it to life with video
steps.text: Send the composite shot to Kling and describe one simple creator movement. Short, natural motion sells it — repeat with new angles for endless variations.
steps.prompt: The UGC creator presents and shows the bag to camera: she lifts it slightly, turns it to show the front, and smiles — natural handheld framing, soft motion, realistic lighting, 5 seconds
steps.result_caption: The output panel in motion. Same actor, same bag, now video.

guides.result: A repeatable pipeline: one AI actor + one product photo = a stream of ultra-realistic UGC ad clips, ready for TikTok, Reels and paid campaigns.

guides.title: Turn a photo into a living particle poster
guides.desc: One photo becomes thousands of dots that scatter under your cursor — a hero page coded by the agent from three prompts.

steps.title: Turn the photo into dots
steps.text: Ask the agent to build a page where your image is redrawn as a halftone grid — thousands of tiny circles, sized by brightness. Pick a photo with strong contrast on a dark background.
steps.prompt: Build a single-page hero section on a pure black background. Center: a photorealistic seashell image rendered as a halftone particle grid — thousands of small circular dots sampled from the image, dot size driven by pixel brightness. Smooth 60fps canvas rendering, subtle floor reflection under the shell.
steps.result_caption: The shell as a dot field. Still a photo — every dot samples one pixel.

steps.title: Make it react to the cursor
steps.text: Add the hook: dots near the cursor fly away with soft physics and drift back when you leave. This one interaction is what makes people stop and play.
steps.prompt: Add interaction: when the cursor moves across the image, nearby dots scatter away with soft spring physics and slowly drift back into place when the cursor leaves. Keep the motion smooth and organic — no jitter, no lag.
steps.result_caption: Cursor moves across, dots scatter and settle. The reaction is what step 2 wired in.

steps.title: Frame it like a poster
steps.text: Finish with an editorial typography layer around the artwork so the page reads as a premium poster, not a tech demo. Then record the page as a video to share.
steps.prompt: Add an editorial typography layer: large serif logotype top-left, small uppercase spaced labels — a tagline top-right, a collection label bottom-left, a "MOVE CURSOR TO DISSOLVE" hint bottom-right, and a small date tag rotated on the left edge. Premium editorial poster look, all text crisp.

guides.result: An interactive particle-poster web page that dissolves under the cursor — recorded here as a 13-second clip, ready for your portfolio or socials.

guides.title: Make a premium product montage
guides.desc: Turn one product into a slick, ad-style video with a few simple shots.

steps.title: Plan the film with one image
steps.text: Generate one storyboard sheet with GPT-Image. It locks the look of every shot before you spend a single video credit.
steps.prompt: A professional film storyboard sheet for a 20-second premium headphones spec ad, dark cinematic layout on black. Eight 16:9 frames in a grid, each with a caption and timecode: box reveal under a single spotlight, hero product floating on black with a specular light sweep, macro of the dial and brushed metal, macro of the knit mesh cushion, person wearing the headphones in a neon city at night, night walk on a wet reflective street, brand end card with the product on a glossy floor, final slow push-in. Consistent silver over-ear headphones in every frame, Apple-style product cinematography, clean typography, high-end pitch deck look.

steps.title: Shot 1 — the reveal
steps.text: Feed the storyboard frame into Seedance and generate the opening clip. One box, one light, nothing else.
steps.prompt: A pristine white product box on a dark reflective floor under one soft spotlight. The lid slowly lifts and warm light blooms from inside, revealing silver over-ear headphones nested in the packaging. Slow overhead push-in, quiet and premium, dark studio, no text.

steps.title: Shot 2 — the hero
steps.text: Now the money shot: the product alone on black with light doing all the work.

steps.title: Shot 4 — the end card
steps.text: Close on the brand, then stitch all four clips together in any editor.
steps.prompt: Silver over-ear headphones stand centered on a glossy black floor with a soft mirror reflection. The camera pushes in slowly while the light gently dims to black. Minimal premium brand end-card mood, elegant and calm, no text.

guides.result: A slick, ad-style product montage ready to post or use as a promo video.

guides.title: Suno obeys your numbers and ignores your structure
guides.desc: The prompt ordered three structural things: a Rhodes-only 4-bar intro that is safe to put a logo over, a dynamic lift in the middle, and a resolved ending. Measured against the delivered file, all three are missing — the bass is playing in bar one, the level moves 2.0 dB across eighty seconds, and the track is faded out mid-groove to land on exactly 90.00 seconds. What it did obey: 85 BPM and the length.

steps.title: The logo-safe intro does not exist
steps.text: "4-bar clean intro (Rhodes only, logo-safe), full groove enters at bar 5" was the whole point of this brief — an editor needs a quiet opening to lay a logo sting over. At 86.1 BPM four bars is 11.2 seconds. Measure the first 2.5 seconds of the delivered file and 28.6% of the spectral energy is already below 120 Hz, with another 31.0% between 120 and 300 Hz: bass and kick are in from bar one. Compare 0:00–0:11 against 0:11–0:22 and the low band barely moves, 22.1% → 24.0%. There is no bar 5 event because there was never an intro. If you need a clean opening, generate the bed and build the intro yourself — take four bars of the track, mute everything but the keys, and butt it onto the front.
steps.prompt: smooth neo-soul jazz R&B ad instrumental, warm Rhodes electric piano, brushed drums, walking upright bass, muted trumpet, elegant and luxurious late-evening lounge, relaxed 85 BPM. Structure for ads: 4-bar clean intro (Rhodes only, logo-safe), full groove enters at bar 5, soft dynamic lift in the middle, calm resolved ending with a short natural tail, no vocals
steps.result_label: The first twelve seconds — supposedly the Rhodes-only intro · 0:00–0:12
steps.result_caption: Full band from the first bar. Nothing changes at 0:11 where bar 5 should be.

steps.title: No lift, no resolve — it runs out of clock
steps.text: Two more structural instructions, both measurable, both missing. "Soft dynamic lift in the middle": sample the level every five seconds and from 0:05 to 1:25 it sits between −11.9 and −13.9 dB — a two-decibel spread across eighty seconds, and an EBU loudness range of 1.8 LU, which is flatter than most podcast dialogue. Nothing lifts. "Calm resolved ending with a short natural tail": at 1:27.5 the groove is still running at −10 dB, then the level falls −21, −23, −28, −40 dB and the file stops at exactly 90.00 seconds. That is not a resolution, that is a fade to hit a duration. Useful, though: an ad bed this flat is genuinely easy to cut into, because no timestamp is louder than any other.
steps.result_label: The last six seconds, no processing added · 1:24–1:30
steps.result_caption: Full groove at −10 dB two seconds from the end, then faded out to land on 90.00 exactly.

steps.title: The cover keeps your palette and ignores your physics
steps.text: Same pattern as the music, in a different medium. The measurable instructions landed: 16:10 exactly (1536×960), one golden light source from the upper left, wine-red and burnt-orange, chiaroscuro falloff. The physical instruction did not — "half-submerged, sinking into the fabric like into thick honey" came back as a trumpet lying on top of draped velvet with the whole bell above the surface, and the "ocean frozen mid-ripple" is ordinary folded fabric. The one thing worth keeping was never asked for: the dark left third is clean enough to hold a title. Describe light, colour and frame and you will get them; describe an object doing something unusual and you will get the object doing the usual thing.
steps.prompt: An experimental surreal album cover artwork for a smooth neo-soul jazz R&B instrumental called "Velvet Hour II", wide 16:10 composition, high-end editorial art photography. Core idea: a brass trumpet half-submerged in a slow-motion ocean of flowing liquid velvet fabric — deep wine-red and burnt-orange silk waves frozen mid-ripple, the trumpet sinking into the fabric like into thick honey. Lighting: single dramatic golden spotlight from upper left, deep wine-red shadow falloff, rich chiaroscuro, photorealistic render with editorial fashion-campaign polish.
steps.result_caption: Palette, light direction and 16:10 frame as briefed. The trumpet is resting on the velvet, not sinking into it.

guides.result: A 90.00-second neo-soul ad bed at 86.1 BPM that sounds expensive and needs two manual edits before an editor can use it: build the logo-safe intro yourself, and replace the timer fade with a real ending.

guides.title: "Brass stabs every 2 bars" landed to within 23 milliseconds
guides.desc: The same model that ignored three structural instructions on the previous track nailed this one exactly: measure the accent cycle in the finished file and it repeats every 4.574 seconds, against 4.551 seconds of theory at 105 BPM. The difference between the instruction that worked and the ones that did not is not effort — it is whether the instruction is a grid or a story.

steps.title: Ask for a cut every 2 bars and you get a cut every 2 bars
steps.text: This is the instruction to copy. "Staccato brass stabs accenting every 2 bars as natural cut points for video editing" is a grid, not a mood — it can only be obeyed one way. Isolate the 2–6 kHz band of the delivered file, where brass transients live, and autocorrelate the onsets: the dominant cycle is 4.574 seconds. At the measured tempo of 105.5 BPM, two bars of 4/4 last 4.551 seconds. The model is 23 milliseconds off across ninety seconds, and the one-bar cycle at 2.287 seconds is almost as strong. That gives an editor a usable cut point roughly every four and a half seconds without touching the audio.
steps.prompt: Confident premium ad instrumental, uptempo jazz-funk R&B groove at 105 BPM. Tight punchy bass line drives throughout, staccato brass stabs (sax and trumpet) accenting every 2 bars as natural cut points for video editing, clean funky electric guitar comping, finger snaps on backbeat. No vocals, polished, energetic but expensive-sounding.
steps.result_label: Exactly three 2-bar cycles from the final track · 0:30–0:43.7
steps.result_caption: Cut to the measured grid, not by ear: 13.72 seconds, three stab cycles, starting and ending on the accent.

steps.title: The same prompt also ordered a breakdown and a hard ending — neither exists
steps.text: Everything in that prompt written as a narrative was dropped. "Breakdown to bass and snaps mid-track": sample the level once a second from 0:40 to 1:06 and it never leaves the −12.8 to −15.8 dB band, with brass energy holding at a quarter to a third of the spectrum throughout — the arrangement never thins out. "Hard clean ending on a downbeat": the groove is still at −16 dB four seconds from the end, then the level falls to −19 and −28 dB and the file stops at exactly 90.00 seconds. Note that number, because it is the same on every track in this set: the model writes to a duration and fades to hit it. Two structural instructions in the same sentence as the grid instruction, and only the grid survived.
steps.result_label: The last six seconds, no processing added · 1:24–1:30
steps.result_caption: Requested: a hard clean ending on a downbeat. Delivered: a fade, timed to land on 90.00 seconds.

steps.title: Why the cover came back perfect and the arrangement did not
steps.text: Check this one against its prompt line by line and there is nothing to report: marble bust cracked open across the chest, tenor saxophone bell erupting through it, fragments suspended mid-air, hard key from the right with warm gold on the brass and cool fill on the marble, charcoal-to-black background, glossy floor reflection, 16:10 at 1536×960. Every instruction landed — and every instruction describes one frozen instant. The music instructions that failed all described change over time: a breakdown in the middle, a hard ending on a downbeat, a lift. The grid instruction worked because it is arithmetic, not narrative. Write image prompts as a single state, write audio prompts as numbers, and build any structure that has to change over time in the edit.
steps.prompt: An experimental surreal album cover artwork for an uptempo jazz-funk R&B groove instrumental called "Brass & Marble", wide 16:10 composition, high-end sculptural art photography. Core idea: a classical white marble statue bust cracked open across the chest — and from inside the cracks, polished brass is bursting out: a gleaming tenor saxophone bell erupting through the shattered marble chest, fragments of marble suspended mid-explosion. Lighting: hard-edged studio spotlight from the right, warm golden key on the brass, cool neutral fill on the marble, dark charcoal-to-black background, glossy floor reflection, photorealistic.
steps.result_caption: Checked against the prompt clause by clause: no deviations found.

guides.result: A 90.00-second jazz-funk bed at 105.5 BPM with a genuine 4.574-second cut grid an editor can rely on — and a cover that matched its brief exactly, unlike the arrangement.

guides.title: Writing "1–4 kHz open" in the prompt bought about 2 dB
guides.desc: The brief spelled out the voiceover range in hertz. Measured against three other beds from the same set, the track that asked sits 2.6 dB quieter in the voice band than the restaurant jazz — and 2.0 dB louder than a track that never mentioned voiceover at all. What actually cleared space for a narrator was a texture word: sparse.

steps.title: "Sparse" produced the intro that "4-bar clean intro" could not
steps.text: One sibling guide in this set asked for a four-bar logo-safe intro in bars and got a full band in bar one. This one asked for nothing structural — just "sparse lonely piano chords with space between them" — and the delivered file opens with thirteen seconds of piano and sub bass running between −18 and −33 dB, with the spectral centroid under 1.7 kHz because there is nothing up top. At 13.0 seconds the arrangement arrives and the level jumps more than 14 dB. That is the largest single event in the track, and nobody asked for it by name. Describe the texture you want and the model will build a shape around it; describe the shape in bars and it will ignore you.
steps.prompt: Intimate minimalist ad instrumental, slow-burn downtempo R&B soul at 70 BPM. Sparse lonely piano chords with space between them, deep soft sub bass, minimal laid-back beat, occasional breathy tenor saxophone phrases, subtle vinyl crackle texture. Arrangement stays open and uncluttered in the 1-4 kHz range so a voiceover can sit on top. Gentle swell in the middle, fades to piano and vinyl noise at the end. No vocals, seductive, calm, expensive.
steps.result_label: The first fifteen seconds, no processing added · 0:00–0:15
steps.result_caption: Thirteen seconds of near-silence, then the band arrives — a 14 dB step you can hear without a meter.

steps.title: The frequency instruction is worth about 2 dB — verify it yourself
steps.text: Band-pass all four beds from this set to 1–4 kHz, the range a narrator occupies, and rank them by median level. This track, the only one that asked: −30.9 dB. Restaurant jazz: −28.3 dB. Jazz-funk: −26.6 dB. The velvet-hour ad bed, which never mentioned voiceover: −32.9 dB, quieter than the one that did. So the instruction is not magic — sparse arrangement and slow tempo are what open the midrange, and a busy arrangement will fill it no matter what you write. It is also not uniformly clear: the loudest voice-band second in this file is at 1:14, at −24.3 dB, roughly six decibels above its own median. Before you commit, run the bed under a real voiceover and duck 1–4 kHz by three or four decibels wherever the narrator speaks.
steps.result_label: The busiest stretch in the voice band · 1:09–1:21
steps.result_caption: Not the calmest part of the track — the loudest, at 1:14. This is where a narrator will fight the sax.

steps.title: Ask for 70% black, measure 91.8%
steps.text: The cover prompt is the one place a percentage appears, and it is the one instruction that overshot: "deep black dominating 70% of the frame" came back with 91.8% of pixels below luma 32. Everything else is exact — vinyl-as-moon with a cold silver rim, a single warm amber beam falling onto an ocean of glossy black piano keys, 1536×960 at 16:10. The overshoot is not a flaw, it is a decision the model made for you: the left third of this image is 99.9% black, which is a title area nobody specified. Treat percentages in image prompts as direction, not as a spec, and check the histogram before you build a layout on top.
steps.prompt: An experimental minimal surreal album cover artwork for a slow-burn downtempo R&B soul instrumental called "After Midnight", wide 16:10 composition, fine-art night photography. Core idea: a vinyl record hanging in a pitch-black night sky as a full moon — its grooves glowing with a thin cold silver rim light, one warm amber beam from the record's center falling down like moonlight onto a vast dark ocean below made of glossy black piano keys stretching to the horizon like water. Lighting: near-total darkness, cold silver rim light on the vinyl moon, one single warm amber light beam as the only warm accent, deep black dominating 70% of the frame, photorealistic, cinematic.
steps.result_caption: Measured, not eyeballed: 91.8% of pixels below luma 32, against the 70% the prompt asked for.

guides.result: 90.00 seconds at 69.8 BPM with a loudness range of 9.0 LU — five times more dynamic than the other ad beds in this set, and the only one whose quiet opening arrived without being asked for. It still fades out to hit the ninety-second mark, so cut the last twelve seconds if you need a real ending.
